How far is too far?
In biomedical research, ethics (moral values) must be considered. Ethics differ between individuals and groups 
of individuals. What one considers acceptable, another does not. Many cultures and religions do not approve of 
‘tampering with nature’, often arguing that humans were not designed to extend life unnaturally. Others argue that 
great minds are meant to be used – hence, if we can find a way to do it, then we should do it! No matter how far we 
progress with scientific research, ethical issues will always be nearby to remind us of other considerations involved 
with developing technology.
Animal Ethics committees are important groups that represent the welfare of animals. In the past, the welfare of 
animals in scientific research was not considered important, and many animals suffered horribly. Today, people 
generally respect the lives (and feelings) of animal subjects used for experimental purposes. Ethics committees are 
often made up of a variety of people, for example, a teacher, a clergyman, several scientists and a police officer. This 
is to ensure a ‘public’ opinion is reached.
1 
Why isn’t the committee made up entirely of scientists? 
 
2 
What sort of questions might be asked of scientists looking for approval to work with animal subjects? Why?
 
3 
‘Right to life’ campaigners believe that people do not have the right to use medical technology to take their 
own lives (humanely) when they are terminally ill. Discuss the ethics of this ‘right’, including reasons for and 
against.

1 
Write each term beside the correct definition: alleles, genotype, heterozygous, homologous, homozygous, 
phenotype, dominant.
a The genetic make-up of an individual organism. 
b Visible physical properties of an organism. 
c Having two different alleles on homologous chromosomes for a characteristic. 
d Different genes that can affect a particular trait. 
e Having the same genes arranged in the same order. 
f Having the same alleles on homologous chromosomes for a characteristic. 
g The characteristic that shows up when there are two competing alleles. 
Usually when there are two alleles for a characteristic, one is dominant and ‘wins’ at being expressed, while the other 
is recessive and ‘loses’. This results in an organism showing one characteristic or the other. The recessive gene is still 
present in the organism, it is just not obvious to the naked eye. 
Take the example of human parents, where one parent has blue eyes and the other has brown eyes. The offspring will 
usually have either two blue eyes or two brown eyes. It is very unlikely that an individual will have one blue eye and 
one brown eye, or eyes that are half brown and half blue – one characteristic is expressed.
Sometimes single genes do not dominate. In co-dominance, both genes are expressed in the physical characteristics of 
the individual. There is not a blend of a characteristic, but a mixture – some of each gene is expressed. 
If a white cow and a red cow mate, there are various possibilities for the colour of offspring.
If conventional dominance occurs, offspring will be either white or red. 
If incomplete dominance occurs, then individual hairs will be mid-way between white and red.

14
Invasive procedures 
In medicine, a procedure is a process carried out on a patient that is designed to lead to an improvement in the 
patient’s health. The procedure can be designed to either investigate or fix a problem. By their very nature, major 
operations are invasive procedures. Any surgical procedure that involves ‘invading’ the body in a way that can lead 
to severe trauma and shock is considered invasive. Examples include: traditional open-heart surgery, which requires 
a large incision to be made in the patient’s chest, followed by breaking open the breastbone; hysterectomies (the 
complete removal of a woman’s uterus); and hip replacements. 
1 
Define trauma and shock, as used above. 
 
2 
List a different example of an invasive procedure. 
Wherever possible, invasive surgery is avoided or modified in order to reduce stress and trauma. For example, 
women who require operations involving the uterus often choose laparoscopy (keyhole surgery) as an alternative 
to a full hysterectomy. Sometimes a full hysterectomy is necessary, for example, to treat cervical cancer and 
endometriosis. 
3 
Women who undergo full hysterectomies require hormone replacement therapy (HRT). What does this tell 
you about the uterus? 
 
Non-invasive and minimally invasive procedures
These either do not involve physically entering a patient’s body or minimise the entry as much as possible. The 
advantages of non-invasive and minimally invasive surgical procedures are great to the patients, the surgeon and the 
tax-paying public. Considerable amounts of money are spent annually on our health system, of which large amounts 
go toward post-operative care (post, meaning ‘after’). The longer a person remains in hospital, the greater the cost 
and the fewer the beds available for other patients.
4 
Discuss the financial and emotional costs involved in hospitalising people.

The term cyborg or cybernetic organism conjures up images of humanoid robots with super-human abilities, 
commonly found in science fiction. Cybernetics is the science of control and communications in animals and 
machines. A cyborg is a ‘blend’ of human and machine. The idea of attaching artificial parts to humans modernised 
the Frankenstein story.  
1 
What is meant by humanoid? 
2 
Suggest why science-fiction writers have often made their characters cybernetic organisms rather than 
‘ordinary’ humans. 
 
3 
List two other fictional cyborgs, and describe how close current technology is to making them possible. 
 
 
4 
Draw and describe a cyborg in your workbook.
The field of Bionics is concerned with developing engineering solutions for impaired (damaged or destroyed) body 
parts. It specialises in creating electrically operated devices to replace or enhance the functions of body parts.  
5 
List six bionic devices and the body part(s) each one repairs or assists. 
 
 
6 
Name a high-profile person who uses (or used) a bionic device. 
Biomaterials and bionic devices
Advances in science and technology have increased our ability to improve, enhance and prolong life using bionic 
devices. By adopting a multidisciplinary approach, biomaterials (materials developed to replace living tissue) have 
been formed to create biomedical devices. A biomedical device is a piece of equipment used for a medical purpose, 
such as helping a person to walk or ensuring a heartbeat remains steady (pacemaker). When biomedical devices are 
implanted within the body, as a pacemaker is, they are called implants. These prosthetic devices have revolutionised 
our approach to illness, injury and disability by taking over, at least in part, the work performed by a damaged or 
destroyed body part.
7 
What do the following define?
a A device designed to correct an anatomical problem

In 1998, the world’s first successful hand transplant was performed (using the hand of a man who died in a 
motorcycle accident). An Australian microsurgeon was one of the team of specialists involved in this ground-
breaking operation. 
The transplant required the usual treatments of immuno-suppressing drugs and other therapies. Immuno-
suppressing drugs restrain (suppress) the immune system so that it doesn’t recognise the ‘non-self’ tissue that is 
transplanted and so doesn’t attack it. This way, the body (often) accepts the ‘foreign’ tissue. However, despite the 
procedure being a technical success, no one foresaw the recipient’s emotional reaction to the surgery. This led to the 
receiver failing to take his medicine and his body completely rejected the transplanted hand. 
1 
The immediate reaction of many people upon hearing this story is surprise that someone who had lost a 
hand wouldn’t be thrilled to have a functional ‘living’ replacement. What sort of emotional problems do you 
think the recipient experienced? 
 
 
2 
For many years, science fiction stories have discussed the use of cryogenics to ‘deep freeze’ bodies of people 
who are suffering from incurable illness, planning to revive them once a cure is found. List arguments for 
and against the use of this technology. 
 
The artificial heart – A brief history
As early as the 1950s, researchers have worked on developing prototypes to replace a diseased heart. This device 
would have to be comfortable, not too large and constructed of materials unlikely to cause blood clotting. Since it is 
preferable that a patient does not undergo multiple operations, the device should also require little maintenance. The 
heart must also be able to respond to the requirements of the recipient, speeding up and slowing down as needed 
and be fully contained (sealed inside) to reduce the risk of infection.

Any artificial device that is designed to replace a living body appendage is called a prosthetic limb. The limbs they 
can replace include arms, legs, feet and hands. 
1 
Define appendage. 
Wooden crutches, ‘peg’ legs and metal ‘hand’ hooks date back to the mid 1700s, and are early examples of prosthetic 
limbs. Peg legs replaced lost legs, and to stop bleeding, arteries were severed after the leg was removed. In the case 
of bleeding arteries, the peg was often screwed into the artery, a painful and dangerous practice. Other peg legs  
were removable and attached by straps. Today, depending on the cause of limb loss, some prosthetic limbs can be 
connected to undamaged muscles, and the muscle’s natural ‘circuitry’ used to operate the myoelectric (myo, meaning 
‘muscle’) prosthetic limb.
2

3 
Apart from working in a similar manner to the missing limb, list other factors that must be considered 
in manufacturing an artificial limb such as a leg, hand or arm. Consider cosmetic reasons – why might 
appearances matter? 
4 
Are crutches considered to be prosthetic devices? Explain your answer.  
 
Shunts and valves – To shunt something means to divert, or redirect it. Shunts are tiny tubes that are used to 
bypass weak, damaged or blocked areas. In the case of living organisms, these areas are usually veins or arteries. For 
example, if a blood vessel has been damaged, a shunt can be inserted to allow blood flow to continue and prevent the 
vessel from rupturing or remaining blocked.  
5 
What might happen if a blood vessel ruptured? 
 
Lenses – Eye glasses (spectacles) and contact lenses are devices used to correct vision impairment. Lenses come in 
a variety of shapes and curvatures, designed to correct the defect in the patient’s eye.

Recombinant DNA 
23
The word recombinant comes from ‘to recombine’ or ‘to combine again’. 
Recombinant DNA is made by splitting DNA molecules and then 
‘splicing’ together specific DNA fragments from two or more DNA 
fragments. In other words, recombining fragments to produce a new 
combination.
DNA can recombine naturally, as it does during the joining of two haploid 
cells. However, recombination can also be achieved artificially.
This technique has given biologists a greater understanding of the make-
up of genes and how they function. A simplified sequence of the process is

Note that in biology, a vector can be an organism that carries and transmits 
disease. In genetics, it is a carrier piece of DNA.
The donor DNA and the vector (usually a plasmid from bacteria) are split 
using microbial enzymes (endonucleases). The highly specific nature of 
these enzymes causes the cut ends of both sets of DNA pieces to match.

sequence of ATAT, what will be the sequence of the sticky end of 
the open plasmid?
 
The ‘foreign’ gene sample is spliced into the open plasmid, which is then  
re-joined using DNA ligase.

This modified plasmid is put into a bacterial cell, such as E. Coli. The 
recombinant DNA is reproduced exactly inside the bacterium cell. This 
cell then divides to form genetically identical copies (clones) through its 
normal replication process. The altered plasmids are then removed from 
the bacterium cell. Using the original restriction enzyme, these plasmids 
are again split and the genes copied from original donor DNA are 
obtained in large quantities.

For a person to be in good health, the heart must beat steadily and blood must flow continuously through it. At rest, 
the heart generally beats around 70 times a minute, governed by electrical stimuli generated by a region of the heart 
called the sinoatrial (SA) node. Sometimes these stimuli do not occur in the regular manner, and this can cause 
heart problems. Until about 40 years ago, major surgery was the only option for people with heart problems. The 
development of non-invasive and minimally invasive medical techniques has been of great benefit to patients.
1 
Outline some advantages of non-invasive and minimally invasive medical techniques over earlier methods. 
 
One of the most familiar biomedical devices is the artificial cardiac pacemaker. It consists of a corrosion-free lithium 
battery and a pulse generator that connects a wire to the heart. It works by sending an electrical charge from the site 
of the SA node. 
The pacemaker came about quite by accident in 1958. While building a device intended to amplify and record the 
sounds made by hearts, American scientist Wilson Greatbatch invented a pacemaker. Modifications were made to 
the original invention, and the pacemaker became a viable proposition. The earliest pacemakers were only partially 
implanted. They had wires that emitted the electrical charge connected to an exterior device. Within ten years, totally 
implantable pacemakers had replaced these versions. In the past, the functioning of pacemakers was affected by the 
wearer standing too close to microwaves, airport metal detectors or other radio-type devices. These difficulties have 
been addressed, leading to the development of the superior models currently in use. 
2 
Suggest risks faced by individuals who used the earliest models of the pacemaker.

The word disease comes from the Latin words dis meaning ‘lack of’ and aise meaning ‘ease’ or ‘comfort’. Whenever a 
virus or other micro-organism impairs (harms, spoils) our health we can be in a state of disease.  
1 
Write each of these terms beside the correct definition below: ailment, hypochondriac, pathogen, epidemiology, 
pandemic, contagious, epidemic.
a Widespread occurrence of disease in an area or country. 
b An illness that can be spread by contact with others. 
c A person who is overly concerned about their health, always thinks they are ill. 
d An illness or medical complaint. 
e Large scale spread of a given disease across the world (global). 
f Study of the spread of disease. 
g A disease-causing microbe. 
There are many causes of disease, including genetics, parasites, viruses, bacteria, sexual transmission and obesity.
Genetic diseases are inherited from one or both parents (who are called carriers). These diseases are ‘programmed’ 
to occur through information coded in our DNA (our genetic material). Most genetic diseases are recessive, 
meaning they require a ‘dose’ of the recessive gene from each parent. The fact that both parents need to donate a 
recessive gene makes many genetic diseases much rarer. Sickle-cell anaemia  is an example of a recessive, blood-
related condition that can be inherited. This disease causes the red blood cells to collapse into a sickle (crescent) 
shape, which reduces the amount of oxygen that can be carried through the body. The cells also tend to clog up the 
blood vascular system which can be dangerous. Genetic diseases are not contagious (not infectious, cannot spread to 
other people).
2 
Why would the fact that both parents need to provide a gene make a condition rarer?

As we can see from the millions of different lifeforms on Earth, organisms have adapted to survive in their  
particular habitats.
1 
Outline what is meant by natural selection and how it relates to adaptation.
These adaptations can be in an animal’s behaviour, structure or physiology (bodily processes). For example, 
migration to a different location to find food or better weather can help a species survive.
2 
Give one other reason for an animal to migrate. 
3 
Name a species that migrates and explain its reasons for doing this. 
4 
The study of the function of the constituent parts of organisms – what does this define?
The owner of some grazing land seeded it with a mixture of grasses and legumes. The pasture was then divided  
into two parts. One part was heavily grazed by cattle and the other part was kept free of livestock and used to 
produce hay. 
After three years, the owner took samples of the grasses and legumes from both parts and re-planted them in an 
experimental garden, ensuring that all samples were exposed to the same environmental conditions. The specimens 
that were taken from the heavily grazed part showed stunted and rambling growth, while those from the ungrazed 
part grew larger and more upright.
5 
Explain why the differentiation in plants occurred, keeping in mind the fact that the same batch of seed was 
used for both parts of the pasture.
Consider the bodily adaptations of marsupials. Kangaroos are terrestrial grazers and their hind limbs are larger and 
more powerful than their forelimbs. The forelimbs of arboreal marsupials (and also those that burrow) are often 
nearly as large as their hind limbs. Kangaroos have large tails, used mainly to help them balance. In tree-dwelling 
species, the tail may also be prehensile.

Diphtheria is a highly contagious disease that 
causes inflammation of the heart and nervous 
system. Prior to the advent of a specific 
antibiotic to treat this disease, the mortality 
rate for people contracting it was about 35%. 
Diphtheria was once widespread but with 
the advent of childhood vaccinations, the 
number of affected individuals has dropped 
dramatically. Antibiotics are only useful 
against bacteria, they do not affect viruses.

one particular country.

When was the antibiotic treatment

your answer.
2

3

Biogeography involves the study of the geographical distribution of animals and plants. This branch of science is 
used to investigate why organisms (plant or animal) are found where they are, and how that affects the land and the 
other species with which they interact. 
Organisms have changed in many ways over long periods of time. Organisms change (evolve) according to 
Darwinian Theory, in response to changes in their environment. The physical location of an organism will affect its 
chances of survival and how it develops, if it survives.

Russell Wallace (1823–1913). In 1839, Darwin published his first accounts of his discoveries from his trip on HMS 
Beagle. He had looked closely at fossils and compared them with living animals in South America and the Galapagos 
islands. Darwin didn’t put forward in detail his long-held beliefs on evolution until 1859, when he saw Wallace’s 
almost identical propositions.

ostriches) varied throughout the South American countries. 
One of his major observations involved the fauna of the

All organisms are composed of microscopic units – cells. The major constituent of most cells is water, H2O. Many 
cells are more than two-thirds water. Water, because it is such a good solvent, dissolves many chemicals and allows 
them to react and move in and out of cells. 
Carbon dioxide (CO2 ) is a gas formed during respiration. It readily dissolves in water and also comes out of solution 
easily. Carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials used by green plants to make complex compounds. Oxygen 
(O2 ) is needed by most organisms. It is not as soluble in water as carbon dioxide is.
1

a Water

Small amounts of minerals (salts) are needed for chemical processes in cells. These minerals include sodium (Na+), 
potassium (K+) and calcium (Ca2+) ions. An ion is an electrically charged particle – that is, a charged atom or group 
of atoms. The attraction between different ions results in chemical reactions and new substances are formed.  With 
the exception of the previously mentioned examples, most of the molecules present in cells are based on the element 
carbon (C), and are called organic compounds.
Glucose, C6H12O6 , is a simple sugar or monosaccharide. It plays an important role in energy transformations in 
organisms.
2 
Which elements are present in glucose? 
3

Glucose is a carbohydrate; it contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Hydrogen and oxygen are in the same ratio as

Matthias Schlieden (1804–81), stated in 1838 that plants are composed of cells. Theodor Schwann (1810–82), a 
German physiologist, advanced a theory in 1839 that animals were also composed of cells. Schlieden and Schwann

white (visible) light and glass lenses. The electron microscope uses a beam of

By the 1880s, microscopes existed that had magnifications in the range of 500  
to 1000 times and very good resolution. Many parts of cells are transparent and  
are difficult to see. 
Scientists developed methods to increase the contrast between parts of cells. 
One method used was to add a dye to a cell. Not all parts of the cell take up the dye to the same extent, and some 
cell structures become coloured more strongly than others.
Staining cells with dye kills the cells, which means that the processes occurring within cells cannot be monitored if 
the cells are stained. Phase contrast microscopy (introduced in 1934 by the Dutch physicist Frits Zernike) increases 
the contrast between living cells and their surroundings, so staining can be avoided. Electron microscopes can 
magnify up to 100 000 times, but cannot be used to study living things because they look at specimens that are in  
a vacuum.

Biology is the study of living things. Another name for a living thing is an organism. Biologists classify 
(sort) things according to their form (shape) and structure (how parts are arranged). All living things have 
characteristics (features) in common. The characteristics of all living things are: moving, sensing, growing 
(and eventually dying), reproducing, eating, respiring and excreting (discharging) of wastes. All living 
creatures are made of cells. An organism with one cell is said to be unicellular, whereas those with lots of 
cells are multicellular. There are very small living things that can only be seen using a microscope. These are 
known as microbes.

Charles Darwin (1809–1882) and Alfred Russell Wallace (1823–1913) independently developed similar ideas about 
evolution being driven by natural selection. The three major ideas below are fundamental to current theories of 
evolution.
• Characteristics of organisms change over time.
• Changes in organisms are driven by natural selection.
• Individuals of a species can’t evolve, but populations do.
1 
Explain the difference between an individual and a population of a species. 
2 
What is more important, the survival of an individual or the survival of a population? Explain your answer.  
Populations of developed organisms are made up of many individuals that share many important features. However, 
all individuals have their own unique differences. 
3 
For humans, state three:
a similarities. 
b differences. 
Darwin’s On the Origin of Species was published in 1859. Although some of Darwin’s ideas on evolution have been 
replaced, his major proposals are still a good basis on which to form the theory of evolution. These are listed below. 
•  There are many different physical characteristics (phenotypes) present in a population.
• Reproduction causes the numbers of that population to increase.
•  Eventually, the supplies of resources will not support the increasing numbers of a population.
• Those individuals who are better suited to obtain resources will survive.
•  The inherited characteristics of the successful organisms will be passed on to their offspring.
• Different environments will be helpful to different types of organisms.
4 
Identify three possible resources that are in demand by organisms in a particular ecosystem.

Beagle (1831–36), Darwin noticed that although the finches in the Galapagos Islands were very similar, they had

33
An ecosystem consists of communities of organisms and the physical environment in which they live. (Remember, 
populations are groups of individuals belonging to the same species, and communities are the sum of the different 
populations living in a given area.) 
All life on Earth is dependent on energy from the Sun. Green plants produce energy by photosynthesis. They are 
autotrophs; that is, they produce their own food from non-living (inorganic) components.
1 
Write another name for autotrophs.                                                         
Animals, fungi and most micro-organisms are unable to use directly the molecules that are present in non-living 
substances. They rely on plants to make complex molecules. If these organisms feed directly on green plants (that is, 
are herbivores), we call them primary consumers.  
2 
What do we call an animal that eats a primary consumer? 
A food chain is the sequence of organisms through 
which energy (and materials) flow in a community. 
Figure 1 shows a simple food chain. The arrow means 
‘is eaten by’ or ‘energy is transferred to’.
3 
In this food chain what is the:
a producer?                                       
b tertiary consumer?                                         
Ecologists describe the successive levels of nourishment in 
a food chain as trophic levels. Producers make up the first 
trophic level; primary consumers are the second trophic 
level, and so on. As you progress up through trophic levels, 
generally the organisms become larger and less numerous. 
Food chains do not exist in isolation. They form complex 
linkages called food webs. Figure 2 shows a simple food web.

producers and consumers involved with these 
organisms? Explain your answer.

Biologists sometimes group organisms according to whether they can maintain a steady body temperature 
independent of external temperatures, or whether their body temperature varies with the external temperature. 
Endotherms (previously known as ‘warm-blooded’ or ‘homeotherms’) are animals such as birds and mammals that 
get their (steady) body warmth from their cell metabolism. (Endo means ‘internal’.) Ectotherms (‘cold-blooded’ or 
‘poikilotherms’) include animals such as reptiles and fish that control their body heat by mainly external means. (Ecto 
means ‘outside’.)

Organisms need many things to survive and reproduce. The things that are used by organisms are called resources. 
The resources for a plant might include sunlight, water, soil and minerals in the soil. Animals need plants for food, 
water to drink, and oxygen to breathe.

resources that there will be pressure on a particular organism for survival. Below is a simplified version of Charles 
Darwin’s Theory of Evolution, caused by natural selection.
• Not all organisms in a population are identical.
•  Organisms that survive for long enough, reproduce and pass on characteristics to their offspring.
• Some characteristics are more useful in a particular environment.
•  The organisms that are more suited to a particular environment are more likely to survive.
•  Over a large number of generations, organisms may evolve to suit their environment.

The belief that living things have changed over time existed well before Charles Darwin (1809–1882) publicly stated

Understanding Biology  – Ecosystems and living things

Exobiology (also called astrobiology) is the study of the origins, evolution and distribution of life within our universe, 
not just on the planet Earth (exo meaning ‘outside’). NASA’s exobiology program is an example of one of several 
organisations actively investigating this mystery. The interest taken by institutions like NASA has given the field a 
new respectability. It is believed the question of the origins of life can best be answered by dividing it into the study 
of the four main parts listed below:
• Prebiotic evolution (pre meaning ‘before’, biotic meaning ‘living/life’)
• The evolution of biogenic compounds (How did they originate?)
• Early evolution of living organisms (e.g. How did life arise and evolve?)
•  Evolution of more advanced organisms (e.g. Does life exist on other planets? If so, is it more/less advanced 
than life on Earth?)
Note that other groupings than the above have been made, but we will only consider the above.
The main elements of life are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorous and sulphur (commonly abbreviated 
as CHONPS). We usually think of these elements as making up Earth’s life forms, but they are also part of the make-
up of the planets, stars and other space matter. Because of this, there is every reason to believe that other life forms 
exist in our universe, since it is so large. 
Scientists have traced the origins of the elements as far back as coming from stars. From there, they went on to form 
planets and other space matter. What we don’t know is where the elements came from in the first place, in order 
for the stars to be formed. This is one of the many mysteries scientists are trying to solve. With so many different 
compounds in existence, there are many pathways to investigate.

The common house mouse has the scientific name Mus domesticus. It is an introduced species. Mice can cause huge 
amounts of damage to crops, equipment and buildings. The cost is estimated to be hundreds of millions of dollars 
per year in Australia, increasing in times of plague. Mouse plagues occur because mice can breed very rapidly if food 
is plentiful and weather conditions are fine. Female mice give birth to a litter (on average, 5 young) less than 3 weeks 
after mating. They can become pregnant almost immediately after giving birth.

© Wendy St Germain, Peter Gribben and Blake Education 2008
44
Biodiversity refers to the total range of organisms (including their genetic information) in a particular habitat. Most 
scientists believe that biodiversity is essential for human life to survive on Earth. The greater the range of species 
in an ecosystem, the greater the chance that this ecosystem will survive sudden changes such as fire or drought. 
Grasslands that have many different types of flora recover more quickly from grazing than similar areas with just a 
few species of plants. 
In the 1840s, a large proportion of Ireland’s population was dependent on 
potatoes for food. Almost the entire potato crop then came from just two 
varieties. In 1845, a fungus (Phytophthora infestans) arrived in Ireland from 
North America. This fungus infected the Irish potato crop causing a blight 
(type of disease) that destroyed the potatoes. The next four years saw the 
continuing failure of the potato harvest due to blight. It is estimated that 
over a million people died of starvation or diseases related to the famine that 
resulted.
Many scientists today are worried about farmers using only one or two 
varieties in their crops or livestock. They are concerned that a disease could 
wipe out a region’s entire production of food if there is a reliance on a few 
types of organisms, instead of a wide range. People raising plants and animals 
as a business are under great pressure to grow these as efficiently as possible. 
There is a temptation to concentrate only on a single breed which may grow  
more quickly or give a greater yield than other breeds.
The clearing of rainforests, bush and other natural habitats is reducing biodiversity. Many wild plants (and animals) 
are in danger of becoming extinct. It is becoming more common for seed banks to be set up by geneticists to ensure 
the conservation of some endangered species. Seed banks store seeds at low temperatures

Division of the heart, by a septum, allows for well-organised movement of blood and produces the effect of two 
separate pumps. From this arrangement, two circulation paths have evolved. These paths are called the systemic and 
pulmonary circuits.
Systemic circuit
Once the exchange of carbon dioxide for oxygen has occurred (at the tiny capillaries of the lungs) the flow of blood 
progresses to the four pulmonary veins (one pair per lung). All freshly oxygenated blood begins its journey through 
the circulatory system at the pulmonary veins, which empty freshly oxygenated blood into the left side of the heart. 
This blood flows to the left atrium and into the left ventricle, which sends it through the aorta to the rest of the body.
1 
Why is the cardiac tissue forming the ventricles thicker than that of the atria? 
 
2 
Although the ventricles are thicker than the atria (overall), the muscles on the left side of the heart are often 
thicker than those on the right side of the heart. Suggest why.
 
Pulmonary circuit 
The right side of the heart contains oxygen-poor blood on its way to the lungs. Fully circulated blood (carbon-
dioxide rich, oxygen poor) travels via the inferior vena cava and superior vena cava into the right atrium. From the 
right atrium, it enters the right ventricle. Blood leaves the right ventricle by the pulmonary arteries. Completely 
deoxygenated blood is only found in the pulmonary arteries. The pulmonary artery branches into two, directing 
blood to the left and right lungs. At each lung the artery divides 
and divides into ever smaller vessels, which eventually become 
capillaries. All this capillary branching creates a greater surface 
area so larger volumes of blood can efficiently replace carbon 
dioxide with oxygen, by bringing it to the surface of the tissue.

Asexual reproduction involves only one parent. The parent 
duplicates its own genetic material, followed by the rest of the 
cell contents. The cell then divides to produce offspring known as 
daughter cells, which are genetically identical to the parent. Clones 
can be defined as plants or animals grown from a single cell or 
plants grown from a single multicellular plant. Clones can also be 
defined as a group of organisms that are genetically identical.
Cloning can be used by humans to grow plants when it is difficult 
to get plants to grow ‘normally’, for example, when seeds are 
difficult to obtain, when mass production of genetically identical 
plants is desired and to increase numbers of a plant threatened by extinction. The Wollemi Pine is an example 
of a plant that exists only in minute numbers. Thought to have died out millions of years ago, a small number of 
specimens were discovered in 1994 and since then scientists have been trying to increase its numbers. Seeds have 
been collected, but only a very small percentage of these have proved viable. Scientists have also tried to increase 
the numbers of Wollemi Pine by taking cuttings and by using tissue culture. In tissue culture, a small piece of tissue 
is taken from a growing part of the plant (e.g. a bud or root). This piece of tissue is then cultured in a medium 
containing the required nutrients. The cells in the tissue replicate and a group of cells is formed. These are treated 
with plant hormones and develop into seedlings. These seedlings are clones of the original parent. They can then be 
grown into plants.

The term ‘ethics’ is derived from the Greek word ethika, which can be loosely translated as ‘the proper conduct, 
customs, principles or standards of how humans should behave’. 
Stem cells are undifferentiated cells (cells that have not yet committed to developing into a specific tissue type). They 
are present in developing embryos. They also occur in adults, but in lesser numbers. If stem cells are removed before 
they follow specific growth patterns, researchers can direct their course of development. It is hoped that stem cell 
research will one day allow replacement organs to be grown for impaired individuals, and help sufferers of diabetes, 
Parkinson’s disease and many other conditions. 
Embryonic stem cell research is extremely controversial, because the cells can be obtained from aborted foetuses. 
Many people are concerned by the idea that our society could use ‘crops’ of embryos in order to help or save other 
people. They think that abortion rates may increase, justified ‘in the name of research’, and some believe that it takes 
away an embryo’s right to life. Those in favour of embryonic stem cell research point out the benefits to society in 
helping people who have potentially curable conditions.

Adult humans have around 5 litres of blood. Human blood is made up of plasma (over 90% water) and blood cells. 
Plasma is a watery fluid (serum). The blood cells that are transported in the plasma carry nutrients to body cells, 
waste matter from body cells, antibodies, enzymes and hormones. Red blood cells make up 99.9% of blood cells – 
platelets and white blood cells make up the remainder. 
Most oxygen is transported through the body bound to haemoglobin in red blood cells. Haemoglobin is a type of 
protein. Only about 2% of oxygen is transported in plasma. When blood clots, the watery plasma separates from the 
cells and the resulting cellular substance forms the clot.

colour to haemoglobin that has no oxygen attached (deoxyhaemoglobin). When light of specific wavelengths is

1 
Read the following passage and explain what is meant by each term in bold (listed below).  
Australian conditions are not always ideal for the growth of seedlings. There can be prolonged drought, high 
temperatures and bushfires. In order for plants to germinate at the ‘correct’ time, i.e. have the greatest chance 
for the seeds to eventually grow into plants, many seeds remain dormant until special conditions occur. The 
mechanisms that inhibit seed from germination can be a chemical present or a thick seed coat. Often people who 
wish to germinate native Australian seeds have to replicate the conditions of the plant’s natural habitat.
Some seeds have a hard seed coat and this needs to be abraded using a substance such as sandpaper. Seeds with 
their coats treated in this way germinate more quickly than untreated seeds.   
Seeds (such as members of the Acacia species) can also be treated by immersion in boiling water. Many seeds 
from areas that are prone to grass fires may need to experience direct exposure to fire and smoke. Fire-activated 
seeds are particularly interesting. A fire must reach a certain intensity before the seed coat will burst open. The fire 
that achieves this intensity will also have been severe enough to destroy the parent plant. This strategy prevents 
seedlings from competing with parents. It also ensures that the species will survive after a severe fire. 
The chemicals preventing germination can be removed by a process called leaching. Here the seeds are suspended 
in a solution and the chemicals are gradually extracted from the seeds.

The average adult brain weighs about 1.4 kg and fills most of the space in the skull (cranial cavity). Of all the body’s 
organs, the brain is the most complex. We can explain how the heart, liver, kidneys and other major organs function, 
but there is still much about the brain and how it works that we don’t understand.  
1 
Brainstorming – We know less about how the brain works than any other organ. Suggest possible reasons 
for this. 
 
We rely on the brain to quickly process and/or recall information. If you walk into your house at dinner time and 
smell fried onions and meat, you know, without seeing it, what you will have for dinner.   
2 
List three other things that we take for granted, thanks to the brain. 
 
Alcohol and the developing brain
Alcohol and cigarettes are known for their damaging effects on the health of their users and on the health of 
developing embryos. We also know that abuse of these substances leads to the destruction of brain tissue (and the 
tissues of other major organs). However, evidence now suggests that these substances are damaging to the brains of 
adolescents and teenagers in a way previously unrealised. Until the age of eighteen years, the brain is still undergoing 
various stages of development with much of the ‘wiring’, in the form of neurones, yet to be completed – or indeed, 
many of the neurons are yet to be created. For this reason, the brain of an individual this age has often been referred 
to as ‘a work in progress’.  
3 
It is illegal to sell alcohol or cigarettes to individuals under the age of eighteen. Why? 
 
What is a neuron?
If you consider the brain as the supercomputer of the Central Nervous System (CNS), then neurons are its wiring. 
Most adult (human) brains contain about 10 billion neurons (neuro, meaning ‘to do with nerves and the nervous 
system’). 
Neurons are specialised cells that differ from oth

The nervous system uses electrical impulses to control the body. There is another important control system – the 
endocrine system. This system works (more slowly than the nervous system) by releasing chemicals called hormones. 
Hormones are special chemical ‘messengers’ which control various activities inside an organism. Human hormones 
are secreted by endocrine glands in response to their environment. Some hormones only act on specific body parts; 
others cause a more general response. Areas in which hormones exert their effects are reproduction, growth and 
development, control of the internal environment and regulation of energy production.
1 
What transports hormones from their point of manufacture to where they are used? 
 
The output of a hormone is usually regulated – the effects they produce often slow down or stop output of the 
hormone.  
2 
Write the name of a process by which output of hormones can be regulated. 
Many hormones are released in response to stress, while others show a daily (circadian) pattern, often peaking  
in the early morning, probably to prepare the body for the stress of getting up.  Aldosterone (a corticosteroid)  
has the formula C21H28O5. It helps in the regulation of the salt and water balance of the body by affecting  
proximal tubules.
3 
Name the main elements present in aldosterone.
 
4 
Which organ contains proximal tubules? 
Aldosterone is secreted by the adrenal gland. There are two adrenal glands – one on each kidney.
The level of hormone changes in response to changes in blood pressure and the levels of electrolytes such as sodium 
(Na+) and potassium (K+) in plasma. If the kidneys excrete too much sodium, an excess of body fluid is also lost. 
Heart function can be affected if potassium levels go outside certain levels.
5 
Electrolytes are ions. What is an ion and how do ions help with reactions?

Understanding Biology – human and plant life
© Wendy St Germain, Peter Gribben and Blake Education 2008
24
The female reproductive system has several functions. It is designed to produce female gametes, called oocytes (more 
commonly called eggs) and to produce important hormones that are required for the normal growth and development 
of the female. Unlike the male system, the female reproductive system is also designed to house and nourish the 
fertilised egg as it develops into an embryo until the woman gives birth. 
Eggs originate in the paired ovaries. The ovaries are round organs which are essential to reproduction (Latin ovum, 
meaning ‘egg’). Approximately every month, the ovaries produce and release an egg (sometimes more than one). 
The ovaries are also responsible for producing the important sex hormones oestrogen (also spelt ‘estrogen’) and 
progesterone. Oestrogen produces the changes necessary for girls to develop into women, and triggers the onset of 
menstruation.  
When a fertilised egg is divided into two, identical twins result. Sometimes the ovary releases two eggs at once and 
each is fertilised by a different sperm. 
1 
Research – What name is given to the twins that result from this second process? 
2 
Why are these twins not identical? 
An egg is released from an ovary on a regular basis, usually every 21 to 28 days, depending on the individual. It 
then travels along the oviduct (Latin ductus, ‘to lead’; also called uterine tube or Fallopian tube) where it can be 
fertilised with the male sperm if it is present. 
The ends of the oviducts have funnel-shaped, almost flower-like, projections (called fimbriae) which catch the 
egg and draw it in. Once inside, the egg travels along the oviduct, where fertilisation usually takes place. Over the 
period of the month, the lining of the uterus, called endometrium, gradually thickens. If fertilisation did not occur, 
the lining is shed and a new one begins to develop shortly after. This monthly cycle

The male reproductive system produces male gametes (sex cells) called sperm (spermatozoa), as well as important 
hormones that are required for normal growth and development. The phase from childhood into adulthood, in both 
sexes, is called puberty. In producing gametes, the male reproductive system must also produce the fluids, ‘foods’ 
and other important components required for the sperm to be healthy and viable. This fluid is called semen. 
During puberty for both sexes, there are many obvious physical changes that occur.
1 
Describe three physical changes that might occur when a male is passing through puberty. 
 
 
Sperm originates in paired organs called testes (singular testis). Compared with the female gamete (oocyte or ‘egg’) 
a sperm is tiny. Testes are housed in a muscular sac called the scrotum. Sperm’s streamlined shape is designed 
to transport one half of the father’s genetic material (DNA) to the egg for fertilisation – as quickly as possible. 
Therefore it contains a DNA-packed ‘head’, the top half of which is covered by a cap. The cap is made of enzymes 
(biological catalysts) which will help to dissolve the outer coating of the egg, thereby allowing the DNA to be taken 
into it. The mid-piece contains mitochondria, organelles whose function is to provide energy for a cell. The sperm’s 
tail is used to propel it through the female reproductive tract, using mitochondria to produce its energy.
2 
Define gamete.

called seminiferous tubules (seminiferous, 
meaning ‘seed-bearing’). Sperm originates 
in the walls of the seminiferous tubules. 
The sperm cells become progressively more 
mature as they move toward the centre of 
the tubule. (See figure 1.) By the time the 
sperm reaches the centre of the tubule, it has 
a tail with which to propel it but it must still 
travel up to the nearby epididymis in or

You may need a text book to help with this section
The nervous system connects every part of the body to the brain by nerves. The brain controls the body – it sends 
(and receives) signals along these nerve fibres. The electrical impulses sent along the nervous system travel very 
quickly, e.g. from the big toe to the brain in a few thousandths of a second. Nerves can be very short or over a metre 
long. The nerves along which signals travel are made up of bundles (varying from a few hundred to a few thousand) 
of long, thin cells called neurones.  
Neurones are specialised nerve cells that transmit signals by electro-chemical changes in their membranes. They 
are ‘long distance’ nerves. There are three major types of neurones – sensory neurones, motor neurones and 
interneurones. Neurones are made up of a cell body, nucleus, axons, dendrites and protective and supportive 
structures. The gap between the axon of one neurone and the dendrite of the next is called a synapse. Electrical 
impulses ‘jump’ across each synapse.  
1 
Draw a diagram showing the cell body, nucleus, myelin sheath, axon and dendrite of one neurone and a 
synapse and the dendrite of the next neurone. 
2 
Write your own definition for nerve (in biology terms). 
 
Dendrites are short extensions of the cell body. They receive stimuli and carry them to the cell body. Axons are 
much longer and there is usually only one axon per neurone. The axon carries nerve impulses away from the cell 
body to other cells. Axons are branched. When an impulse reaches the end of the axon branches, chemicals are 
released (neurotransmitters) to the dendrite of the next cell. When the neurotransmitter reaches this dendrite, a fresh 
electrical signal is generated and this travels through this next cell, and so on.

32
An organ system is a collection of tissues or organs that work together, each with a specific task (or tasks) related 
to the healthy functioning of an organism. Plants and animals both have organ systems (Latin organum, meaning 
‘tool, instrument’). Plants have two main organ systems – one works below the ground, the other above ground.  
1 
Name the organ system that works below ground. 
2 
Name the organ system that works above ground. 
Roots, tubers and rhizomes form the plant’s underground organ system. 
Roots are usually (but not always) found underground. Their function is to 
absorb water and nutrients for the plant’s growth and development. Roots 
also store excess sugars and act as anchors, holding the plant in place and 
giving it stability as it grows. Tiny root hairs grow off roots to increase the 
roots’ surface area.
Tubers act like a pantry. They store food for the plant. Buds are often 
present on tubers (tuber comes from a Latin word meaning ‘swelling’ or 
‘knob’). 
Rhizomes are underground stems that grow horizontally (creep along) 
underground. Rhizomes grow roots and also store food, allowing a plant to 
spread across an area. Shoots, leaves, flowers and fruits are examples of a 
plant’s above-ground organs.
3

14
The nervous system uses electrical impulses to control the body. The 
nervous system is necessary for instant communication and reaction. 
The communications are short, fast and tend to be limited to a small 
area. It is an important control system but not the only one. 
There is another important control structure – the endocrine system. 
This is a slower system, with longer term effects. The endocrine system 
is a network of glands (and cells) in animals that send hormones (Greek 
hormaein, meaning ‘to set in motion, to move’) throughout the body. 
Plants do not have an endocrine system. 
Hormones are ‘chemical messengers’ that cause or prevent specific 
reactions. Areas in which hormones exert their effects are reproduction, 
growth and development, control of the internal environment and 
regulation of energy production. Some hormones, such as those 
produced in the thyroid gland (and growth hormones), affect all the cells 
of the body, not just limited targets.    
1 
What do the nervous system and the endocrine system have in 
common?
 
2 
Name two differences between the nervous system and the 
endocrine system.
 
 
3 
Name three areas over which hormones exert an influence. 
 
Hormones are secreted (released) by glands into the bloodstream which then carries them to the target sites. Figure 
1 shows the location of the major glands (and some other organs). Hormones control and regulate the body’s 
activities by sending messages to tissues, cells or organs. Only small amounts of hormones are required to perform 
these functions. Hormones have specific protein receptors or sites to which they bond. The receptors can ‘recognise’ 
what they must bond to as they travel through the bloodstream. When bonding occurs, a reaction is triggered.
The pituitary gland is sometimes called the ‘master gland’ because the hormones it secretes affect so many other 
glands.

The human heart 
1
The heart pumps blood around the body and is one of the first organs to function in an embryo.  
1 
What is an embryo? 
The heart circulates blood through the body. The vessels carrying the blood throughout the body are capillaries 
(narrow), veins (medium-sized) and arteries (large). A human’s heart is roughly the size of their fist; for example, a 
five-year-old child’s heart is roughly the size of that child’s fist. The heart is made of muscle tissue called myocardium 
(myo, meaning ‘muscle’). The heart is powered by the sinoatrial (SA) node. The SA node gives a small charge to the 
tissue, setting the pace of the heartbeat.
Wrapped around the heart is a protective covering, the pericardium (peri, 
meaning ‘around’). This is a sac-like membrane. The pericardium acts like  
a special ‘cling wrap’ around the myocardium. 
The heart is divided into four chambers (compartments), two upper and two 
lower. The left and right sides of the heart are divided by a septum (septum, 
meaning ‘enclosure’ or ‘fence’) which acts like a wall between the two halves. 
Each chamber of the heart is either an atrium (plural atria) or a ventricle.  
2

arrive. Atrium is an old-fashioned word used to describe the central  
court of ancient Roman homes. Therefore, for the heart, would the 
atrium/atria refer to the top chambers or the bottom chambers?

The kidneys 
5
The kidneys are the two main organs of excretion. Excretion is the process of removing waste from the body. Your 
kidneys are paired and each is about the size of your fist. They are found in the lower back on each side of the spine. 
The left kidney is located just under the liver and the right kidney is not far from the spleen. Because the liver is large 
and needs more space, the left kidney is a little bit lower than the right. Kidneys filter blood, removing unwanted 
substances. As part of homeostasis they regulate the level and contents of body fluids. 
Blood filled with impurities is carried to the kidney by the renal artery. The renal 
artery branches into smaller arterioles and then into capillaries which will later 
join together to empty purified blood back into the renal vein. The outer part of 
an organ is called the cortex and the inner part is called the medulla. Nephrons are 
the filtering units of the kidney. They are housed in hollow cavities in the medulla. 
Nephrons are tiny units and there are approximately one million in each kidney. 
Each nephron is made up of a renal corpuscle and a kidney (uriniferous) tubule.

sac surrounding the glomerulus). Blood is made of cells and plasma. Plasma makes up about 55% of blood’s 
composition. It is a straw-coloured substance made mostly of water, containing inorganic salts, proteins and other 
substances.

The liver is the largest of the major internal organs. It is located (roughly) under the bottom of the right side of your 
ribcage. The average human liver weighs just over 1.5 kg and is a dark brownish-red colour. It consists of a large 
right lobe and a smaller left lobe. The liver is involved in digestion, metabolism and detoxifying the body (removal of 
toxins). 
1 
Define toxin. 
The liver produces a substance called bile. Bile is used to break down fats 
(and fat-soluble vitamins) by emulsifying the foods we eat. Bile is a brownish-
green, bitter substance. It is stored in the gallbladder. 
2

4

A good way to picture the liver is by imagining strings of cotton reels suspended in fluid. Each cotton reel represents 
a cell and there are many of these cells suspended in a pool of blood.
5 
If you squeeze a piece of raw liver between your fingertips you will see how easily it collapses. What does 
this tell you about the cells?
There is a lot of activity going on among the ‘strings’ of liver cells. They work with the immune system and also 
play an important role in managing how our blood clots. When the liver is damaged, these strings of cells harden 
and become useless scar tissue. Fats and fat-soluble substances accumulate in our bodies, as do toxins, bacteria and 
germs. Without our livers, we would soon drown in our own poison. Liver failure kills.
6

activities mean?

The word transpiration comes from the Latin trans meaning ‘across’ or ‘through’ and spirare which means ‘to 
breathe or pass something through pores or tissue’. Transpiration is the word used to describe the loss of water 
from a plant, in the form of water vapour. The water is lost through tiny pores in the leaves. These pores are called 
stomata. The singular form of stomata is stoma, meaning ‘mouth’. Under the microscope, a stoma looks a bit like 
a little mouth, with lips that open and shut. Usually stomata open at sunrise and close at night. (Although some 
desert plants have stomata that open at night.) Therefore stomata, like the chloroplasts described below, are also 
activated to a large degree by sunlight.
1 
Write another word for vapour.                                            
Throughout the day, stomata open and close as the plant requires. When the plant is low on water, they close to 
prevent further water loss, although a certain amount is still transpired. When water is readily available, stomata 
open. In average conditions, over 90% of the water a plant takes up through its roots is transpired. 
All vascular plants transpire. Vascular means ‘vessel’. Vascular plants carry water and nutrients (dissolved minerals) 
through a system of vessels or ‘tubes’. The vascular system is easily observed by cutting a stick of celery crossways. 
To see transpired water vapour, tie a clear plastic bag over the cut section and leave it for several hours to become 
visible. You should see the colour drawing up the celery. If left for long enough, the leaves will also start taking in 
the colour. 
Plants actively photosynthesise during periods of light. This is when transpiration action is at its greatest. It is 
important not to confuse transpiration with evaporation – they are two different processes.

In modern agriculture, the use of pesticides is necessary. Aerial spraying (‘crop dusting’) is used to cover large or 
inaccessible areas. However, not all of the chemicals sprayed reach their intended sites. It has been estimated that 
about 85% of pesticides delivered in this way can drift tens of kilometres from the point of delivery. 
Many agricultural operations can generate particulate matter into the 
atmosphere during hot, dry weather. Methane (CH4) gas is produced by 
many agricultural activities – the two major sources are rice production and 
ruminant livestock. In one day, a sheep can produce approximately 30 litres 
of methane and a dairy cow up to 200 litres.
People who live in rural areas are not exposed to the same pollutants as those 
who live in cities, but they have to contend with nuisance odours and other 
more toxic airborne pollution.
1 
What is meant by a nuisance odour ?
2 What is meant by particulate matter ?
3 Assuming that there are 28.6 million sheep in Australia, calculate  
how many litres of methane they will produce in a year.
4 If methane has a density of 0.68 g L–1, calculate the mass of methane 
produced by these sheep in a year.
The Greenhouse Effect is the heating of the Earth due to the 
presence of Greenhouse gases. Methane is a Greenhouse gas, 
which means it contributes to the Greenhouse Effect.  
Without the Greenhouse Effect, the Earth’s mean temperature 
would be around 30°C less than it is, and the daily temperature 
would fluctuate much more than it currently does. However, 
many people think that continued emissions of Greenhouse gases 
by human activity will increase the Greenhouse Effect and cause 
Global Warming – the increase of the Earth’s mean temperature. 
Figure 1 shows the relative percentages of Greenhouse gases in 
Earth’s atmosphere.
5 Referring to figure 1, name the Greenhouse gas present in the greatest quantity.

Ionic compounds and macromolecules (e.g. covalent network structures) do not have molecular formulae. Instead, 
their empirical formula is used. This doesn’t give the actual number of atoms present, which could be a very large 
number, but the simple whole number ratio of atoms – the empirical formula of a compound states the relative 
number of each type of atom present. 
When carrying out analysis of the composition of a chemical compound, only the empirical formula can be found. 
A typical quantitative investigation into a compound will reveal either the masses or the relative percentages of 
individual elements present. The procedure for working out the empirical formula is the same in both cases. The 
number of moles of each element present is calculated and then the ratio.

Activation energy (EA) is the energy required for a reaction to proceed. Activation energy is an important concept 
when describing how catalysts work. For particles to react with each other, they must collide with each other for the 
outer electrons to make contact and for bonding to occur.
1 
What is the name for the outermost electrons of an atom? 
In order for reactions to happen, bonds must be broken and the repulsion between electrons overcome. These 
processes require energy, and this energy is called activation energy. Different reactions have different values for the 
activation energy.
2 A reaction takes place spontaneously at room temperature.  
What does this tell you about the activation energy for this particular reaction? 
3 Think of reactions you have carried out that needed an input of energy before they would start.  
Name two reactions and outline how energy was used to ‘start them off’.
Figure 1 shows the reaction profile for an exothermic reaction. In these reactions, the energy level of the products 
is lower than that of the reactants, the enthalpy change (ΔH) is negative and heat is given off. In an endothermic 
reaction, the energy level of the products is higher than that of the reactants, the enthalpy change (ΔH) is positive 
and heat is absorbed.

and label the equivalent diagram  
for an endothermic reaction.
Catalysts speed up the rates of reaction without being consumed (used up)  
at the end of the reaction. They do this by altering the path of the reaction  
and lowering the activation energy required. The overall enthalpy change  
(ΔH) remains the same, only the activation energy (EA) is lowered.

Chromatography is the process of separating small amounts of substances from mixtures by the relative speeds at 
which they move through or along a medium. Chromatography was first used by Mikhail Tsvet in 1901 to separate 
plant pigments. 
1 
Give another term for pigment.
There are many chromatographic techniques, but they all rely on the components of a mixture being carried by a 
mobile phase over (or through) a stationary phase (the medium) at different rates. The molecules in the mixture will 
have different interactions with the stationary phase. The greater the interaction, the slower the substance will move 
through the stationary phase. 
Chromatography is used to identify dyes, additives, pharmaceuticals and many other organic compounds. 
Chromatography is especially useful in forensic chemistry.
2 What is forensic chemistry? 
Paper chromatography uses a liquid solvent as the mobile phase and 
paper as the stationary phase – strictly speaking, it is water absorbed 
by the paper that is the stationary phase. The mixture to be separated 
is dissolved in the minimum amount of a solvent. This is placed on the 
surface of the paper. A second solvent flows across the sample, carrying it 
through the paper. (See figure 1.) Radial chromatography and ascending 
chromatography are the two most common examples.
Figure 2 shows the sequence followed in a simple radial 
chromatography procedure.

ascending chromatography.

a identify the stationary phase.

Many organic molecules have charges or become electrically charged when dispersed in a fluid. If electrodes are 
placed in a fluid containing these molecules then the charged particles will move towards the opposite charges. 
Electrophoresis is the movement of electrically charged particles through a fluid or gel under the influence of an 
external electrical field.
Figure 1 shows the major components used in the 
technique of paper electrophoresis. The mixture is 
spotted onto moist paper, the end of which is dipped into 
buffer solution. A high voltage is applied, causing anions 
and cations to migrate. This type of electrophoresis is best 
suited to the analysis of small molecules.
1 
Define anion. 
2 Define cation. 
3 Why must the paper be moist in paper electrophoresis? 
Gel electrophoresis uses a gel as the stationary medium.  
The gel is porous and smaller particles move through it  
more easily than larger particles do. 
Gel electrophoresis can be carried out either horizontally 
or in columns. It is commonly used to separate and identify 
DNA mixtures. 
Figure 2 shows two views of a typical apparatus used in gel 
electrophoresis. Holes (sample wells) are cut into the gel and 
the mixtures of for example DNA fragments are placed in 
them. Often a dye is added so the progress of the process can 
be observed. Molecular markers, which are mixtures of DNA 
with known molecular masses, are also sometimes added. 
Then a current is applied. 
Because the DNA molecules have a negative charge, they 
are attracted to the positive anode. The greater the charge, 
the greater the attraction. The DNA then has to be treated 
chemically before it can be observed.

In gas–liquid chromatography (GLC), the stationary phase is a liquid coated onto very small particles of inert solid. 
This is packed into a narrow tube which is usually referred to as a column, and is normally coiled to save space and 
made of stainless steel. The mobile phase is an unreactive gas. 
1 
Name two suitable gases that could be used for the mobile phase of GLC. 
A carrier gas (the mobile phase) is allowed to flow through the column until conditions have stabilised. A syringe is 
used to inject the sample into the machine where it is vapourised using a small oven. The carrier gas transports the 
analyte (substance being analysed) mixture through the column. The column is contained in a separate oven, with 
temperatures typically in the range of 50°C to 250°C.
2 Why is the column kept in an oven? 
3 Outline why stainless steel is a good material for making a GLC column. 
The different components of the analyte will interact differently with the stationary phase in the column. This will 
cause each compound to have a different retention time, i.e. the time it spends in the column. These retention times 
are used to identify the substances present. As the components reach a detector, the time of arrival and amount of 
substance is recorded. Levels as low as in the nanogram range can be detected by more sensitive equipment.
4 What is a nanogram?  
GLC cannot always detect 
and conclusively identify the 
components in a mixture, so 
it is often linked to a mass 
spectrometer. The fragmentation 
pattern obtained can be compared 
to others stored in a database.

terms: kinetic, minute, discrete, chaotic, translation, negligible, collision, elastic
•  Gases consist of minute, discrete particles (usually molecules) in continuous,  
chaotic motion and with high speeds.
•  The average speed of motion increases with the absolute temperature, which  
is thus some measure of the average energy of motion, i.e. kinetic energy.  
At absolute zero (0 K), movement from place to place, i.e. energy of translation,  
is at a minimum.
•  Collisions between molecules and bombardment of the walls of the containing 
vessel occur, the latter is the cause of gaseous pressure, which is force per unit area.
•  The collisions are assumed to be perfectly elastic without any loss of energy. 
Otherwise, the pressure of a given amount of gas would alter over time.
•  The distances between the molecules are large in comparison with the size of the 
molecules. At low pressures, molecules may even be considered as point masses,  
i.e. have negligible volume.
•  At low pressures, the forces of attraction between molecules  
are insignificant.

at 101.3 kPa (1 atm) and 0°C occupies 22.4 litres and at 101.3 kPa and 25°C occupies 24.5 litres.

Nuclear chemistry deals with the nuclei of atoms. The nucleus 
contains most of the mass of an atom (protons and neutrons) but 
occupies very little space. Ernest Rutherford first proposed the 
existence of the nucleus in 1911. James Chadwick discovered the 
neutron in 1932. Table 1 shows the properties of the nucleons.
1 
What does amu represent? 
The number of protons present in a nucleus of an atom gives the atomic number of that element. 
2 Suggest why protons and neutrons are referred to as nucleons.
Why does the nucleus hold together? You would expect the positive protons to repel each other. Part of the answer 
involves ‘binding energy’. If you look at the numbers of protons and neutrons in a particular atom and calculate the 
mass the nucleus should be, you will find that the actual mass of the nucleus is less than the theoretical value. The 
‘missing’ mass (mass deficit) has been transformed into ‘binding energy’ which holds the nucleons together. 
Some elements have isotopes, i.e. their atoms will have the same number of electrons and protons, but different 
numbers of neutrons. In 1919, Francis Aston used a mass spectrometer to measure mass and percentages of isotopes 
accurately. Isotopes can be identified by writing the mass number after the name of the element e.g. carbon-14 or 
uranium-235. The mass quoted in data tables is usually the weighted average of the naturally occurring element.
3 Nucleus A has 15 protons and 16 neutrons, whereas nucleus B has  
16 protons and 16 neutrons. Are they isotopes? Explain your answer.

uranium-235 and uranium-238. A Periodic Table gives the  
relative atomic mass of uranium as 238.02. What does this tell  
you about the relative proportions of the isotopes in nature?

• half the nuclei in a sample of a radioisotope to undergo radioactive decay.
• the activity of a sample of a radioisotope to decrease to one half of its original value.

Practical work plays a major part in all Chemistry courses. All practical activities have potential hazards and a risk 
assessment should be carried out before proceeding with any practical work. Your teacher will have completed a risk 
assessment before you undertake any practical activity. However, you are expected to have an awareness of health 
and safety issues relevant to the Chemistry laboratory. 
You should be able to complete the following for practical activities:
• identify possible hazards
• assess the risks that might arise from these hazards
• describe appropriate measures to minimise the risks.
Possible hazards include:
• glassware – can be hot or break when dropped
• chemicals – can be toxic, corrosive, carcinogenic or cause allergic response
• liquids – can be spilt or ‘spit’ from heated mixtures
• solvents – flammable, toxic, narcotic
• naked flames e.g. Bunsen burner
• dust or fumes – can be generated during burning
• water – can be spilt on the floor, making it slippery.

soluble in all proportions (i.e. miscible) with water. Others such as silver chloride are either very poorly soluble or 
insoluble in water.

Solutions are defined as homogenous mixtures; they have particles uniformly spread through the mixture. Although 
solutions will pass through filter paper, like most mixtures, the individual components in a solution can be 
separated.

be slightly polar (e.g. ethanol, figure 3) or non-polar (e.g. benzene, figure 4).

The mass spectrometer was invented around 100 years ago. It is a very useful tool for identifying the presence of 
isotopes of metals and non-metals. It can also be to identify molecular compounds. A mass spectrometer acts as 
a very accurate balance for finding masses. When molecules are put into a mass spectrometer, they can be broken 
down into fragments.
Positive ions (cations) travel through a vacuum and are deflected by electric charge 
and magnetic fields. The degree of deflection can be used to identify the species. 
The amount of deflection depends on the mass of the particle and its charge. 
Here is a sequence followed in a typical mass spectrometer.
Step 1: The (very small) sample is vapourised by heating.
Step 2: The sample is introduced into the ionising chamber.
Step 3: High energy electrons bombard the sample and cause it to form positive ions.
Step 4: The positive ions are accelerated out of the ionising chamber by applying a high voltage.
Step 5: The beam of ions is focused and collimated (turned into a narrow beam).
Step 6: An ‘electrostatic analyser’ deflects cations of a narrow mass range into the magnetic analyser.
Step 7: The electromagnet is adjusted to select cations of a specific mass to hit the detector.
Step 8: The detector produces a small electric current which is amplified and then recorded.
Step 9: The strength of the electromagnet is adjusted to allow more massive cations to be detected.

Transition metals occupy the middle of the Periodic Table, between Groups II and III. They are sometimes known 
as the ‘d-block’ elements. Most definitions classify transition metals as those with incomplete inner d-subshells. 
They don’t follow the normal way of electrons filling shells in sequence. Copper, cadmium and zinc have complete 
d-subshells and so don’t meet this criterion. Copper and cadmium are often included despite this, because they have 
physical and chemical properties in common with the main body of transition metals.

that can exist in differing amounts or types during an investigation. Usually only one variable is changed at a time.

independent variable is changed. 
•  A control (controlled variable) is one that is kept the same in each experiment.

Polluted water is water that is not fit for the purpose for which it is intended. Pollutants in water can include toxic 
chemicals and pathogens. When we refer to ‘water pollution’, we tend to concentrate on contamination that has been 
caused by human activity. 
The manufacturing industry is responsible for a major part of water 
pollution. Many factories discharge polluted water (effluent) into rivers, 
lakes or oceans. Although there are statutory limits on the amounts of 
pollutants that can be in this waste water, total volumes can be huge and 
can severely degrade water quality. Industrial pollutants that enter water 
supplies include heavy metals (e.g. mercury), organic solvents and oils.

(coal, oil or natural gas), use nuclear power or utilise moving water or wind. When coal is burned, it forms sulfur 
dioxide (SO2) which is a major contributor to acid rain. When acid rain falls it enters bodies of water, causing 
them to become too acidic for aquatic life. Both coal-fired power stations and nuclear power stations require large 
amounts of water for cooling. The hot water discharged into rivers or oceans can cause thermal pollution.

Alkenes and alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons. They contain one or more 
double (alkenes) or triple (alkynes) carbon-to-carbon bonds. Those with 
more than one double bond or triple bond are referred to as polyunsaturated. 
Alkenes are named in a similar way to the alkanes, using the suffix ‘-ene’. 
The simplest alkene is ethene, C2H4. Figure 1 shows the three representations 
of the structure of ethene. 
In structural formulae, the carbon-to-carbon double bond is represented by a 
double line. Note that the atoms immediately connected to the carbon-carbon 
double bond lie in a plane. The bond angles are bent well away from the ideal 
value of a tetrahedron. The bond is an area of high electron density and is 
therefore attractive to electrophiles; i.e. reagents that accept electrons.
1 
What does it mean to say a hydrocarbon is mono-unsaturated?  
The next alkene in the homologous series is propene, C3H6. Figure 2 shows its  
structural formula. Once there are four or more carbon atoms in the chain of an alkene,  
more than one structure is possible.

•  The chain is numbered from the end nearer a carbon involved in the 
double bond.
•  The lower of the two numbers identifying the carbon atoms is used to locate the double bond.
•  If more than one double bond is present, the compound is named as a diene, triene, etc.  
Each double bond is assigned a number to locate it.

Alkynes are hydrocarbons that contain a carbon-to-carbon triple bond. They are named in a similar way to alkanes 
and alkenes, but using the suffix ‘-yne.’ Figure 1 shows the three representations of the structure of ethyne (C2H2) 
which has the trivial (common) name of acetylene. 
In structural formula, the carbon-to-carbon triple bond is represented by a triple line. Note that the atoms 
immediately connected to the carbon-carbon triple bond lie in a straight line. In a similar manner to alkenes, the 
bond angles are under severe strain (180° rather than the preferred 109.5°). The carbon-to-carbon triple bond is an 
area of even higher electron density than with alkenes. Because of these factors, the carbon-carbon triple bond is 
extremely reactive. 
Ethyne is the most common alkyne. The major use of ethyne is welding – the phrase ‘oxy-acetylene’ refers to an 
oxygen and ethyne mixture that gives a very high temperature when burning, up to 2 800°C.
1 
Write a word equation and then a balanced formula equation for the combustion of ethyne.
Ethyne can be used to make chloroethene, a raw material used to make PVC, and also 1, 1, 2, 2-tetrachloroethane 
which is a solvent.

decolourise bromine water. Alkanes do not undergo addition reactions and do not decolourise bromine water.

The chemistry of amino acids and proteins looks complex, but a knowledge of the structures of these compounds 
will help. Amino acids are the monomers that make up proteins. The two major functional groups present in amino 
acids are the amine and carboxylic (alkanoic) groups. 
Figure 1 shows the general structure of amino acids. ‘R’ represents a side chain, often an alkyl group. The simplest 
amino acid is glycine, where a single hydrogen takes the place of R.
1

b Give the formula for the carboxylic group.

3 Give the formula for glycine.

4 What is meant by polar ? 
5 The carboxylic group has acidic properties and the amine group has basic properties. 
Outline what is meant by the terms acidic and basic in terms of proton transfer.
When amino acids are in solution, they can dissociate (break apart) as shown in figure 2. 
Notice that the amino acid molecule can simultaneously act as an acid and a base to form a zwitterion. 
6 Study figure 2. Using the information above, devise a general description of a zwitterion.
Overall, the molecule is neutral. However, this structure only 
occurs at a particular pH. In solutions of low pH levels, the 
carboxylate end of the molecule can gain a proton to form a 
positive ion.
7 Using figure 2 as a guide, show how a zwitterion can  
become positively charged when it gains a hydrogen ion.
In solutions of high pH levels, the amine end of the zwitterion can donate  
a proton to hydroxide ions to form water and a negative ion.
8 Using figure 2 as a guide, show how a zwitterion can become negatively charged 
when it loses a hydrogen ion.
9 A chemical compound that is electrically neutral but at  
a specific pH can have positive and negative charges on 
different atoms.

If you add acids or bases – even in small amounts – to water and most solutions, the pH can change considerably. 
Buffer solutions are less susceptible to changes in pH when small amounts of acids (H+) or bases (OH–) are added. 
Buffer solutions are not necessarily neutral; they can be formulated to a wide variety of pHs. They can be used to:
• calibrate pH meters
• maintain an optimum pH for industrial processes e.g. dyeing cloth
• keep pH within a certain range for enzymes e.g. involved in body processes.
An acidic buffer solution contains a weak acid and its salt, often the sodium salt. 
Basic buffer solutions contain a weak base and its salt. Buffer solutions are examples 
of equilibrium systems and a knowledge of Le Châtelier’s principle can help you 
understand how these systems work.
1

2 Name two weak bases. 
3 Outline Le Châtelier’s principle.

(aq) + H3O+
