A buffer solution involving ethanoic acid would have a salt of this acid added,  
e.g. sodium ethanoate, CH3COONa. In aqueous solution this would dissociate as shown:
CH3COONa(s) + H2O(l)  CH3COO–
(aq) + Na+
(aq)
5 Sodium ethanoate is a strong electrolyte. Explain how the dissociation would be affected.
When the equilibrium system is described for the buffer solution made up of ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate, the 
sodium ion is usually omitted because it is regarded as a ‘spectator ion’.
6 Explain what a spectator ion is. 
In this mixture, the acid is almost completely undissociated and the salt almost completely dissociated as shown:

(aq) + H3O+
(aq)

We use calorimetry to measure the heat changes involved in chemical reactions. The term calorimetry comes from 
the Latin calor meaning ‘heat or warmth’. A calorimeter is the apparatus used to carry out calorimetry experiments. 
A calorimeter can be as simple as a styrofoam coffee cup with a thermometer or a very complex device. Figures 1, 
2 and 3 show three common calorimeters used in schools. Calorimetry experiments measure the heat change that 
occurs for a particular chemical reaction using known quantities of reactants. 
1 
Write your own definition for calorimeter. 
In exothermic reactions:
• heat is given out
• ΔH is negative
• the temperature of the system rises then falls.
2 Outline the characteristics of endothermic reactions.
When carrying out calorimetry experiments, we measure the temperature change. When you carry out an 
investigation, ensure that you have measured the maximum temperature change that has occurred. When 
calculating the enthalpy (heat) change (ΔH) involved in a reaction, you need to measure the mass (m), know the 
specific heat (Cp) and measure the temperature change (ΔT) of the system. The enthalpy change is calculated using 
the formula ΔH = mCpΔT; i.e. mass of reactants times specific heat times change in temperature. 
Study the following carefully.
ΔH = mCΔT
ΔH = enthalpy change (joules, J)
m = mass (grams, g)
Cp =  specific heat (joules per gram per degree, Jg–1°C–1) tells us how much  
energy (J) is required to raise 1 gram of the substance by 1°C (1 K)
ΔT = temperature change (degrees Celsius, °C, or kelvins, K)

The theory of proton transfer was developed independently by Brönsted and Lowry. It is a very useful theory for 
accounting for the properties of acids and bases. According to Brönsted–Lowry, an acid is a proton donor and a base 
is a proton acceptor. In aqueous solutions, hydrogen ions are hydrated – i.e. exist as H3O+ (hydroxonium) ions.
Using HA to represent a typical (monobasic) acid, we can show how an acid behaves when it is dissolved.
 
HA(aq) + H2O(l) → A–
(aq) + H3O+
(aq)
The HA has acted as an acid because it has lost a proton. The H2O has acted as a base because it has gained a proton. 
However, this is an equilibrium process and so is written as: 
 
HA(aq) + H2O(l)  A–
(aq) + H3O+
(aq)
Hence the reaction H3O+
(aq) + A–
(aq) → H2O(l) + HA(aq) also occurs.

system. Some species on opposite sides of the equation (HA/A– and 
H2O/H3O+) only differ by a proton (hydrogen ion). We call these 
conjugate acid–base pairs. The conjugate base of the acid HA is A–  
and the conjugate acid of the base H2O is H3O+.

• aliphatic – based on alkanes and alkenes

Enzymes are a special class of proteins that act as very efficient biological catalysts. They have some differences from 
inorganic catalysts, in that enzymes:
• are often very specific in the reactions they catalyse
• only work over a narrow temperature range
• only work over a narrow pH range.
Individual enzymes are named by adding ‘-ase’ onto the name of the substrate with which they reac; e.g. urease 
controls the decomposition of urea. However some have trivial names, such as pepsin.
1 
What is meant by a trivial name ? 
Enzymes have an ‘active site’. This is an area with a particular structure and shape within which the specific substrate 
will ‘fit’. Intermolecular forces hold the substrate in a particular position. The substitute-enzyme complex can either 
decompose or react with another substance. 
Figure 1 shows a possible sequence of an enzyme-catalysed reaction. The substrate diffuses to the active site on the 
enzyme and forms an enzyme-substrate complex. The products then diffuse from the active site.
2 Copy figure 1 and identify the active site, the substrate, the enzyme-substrate complex and the products. 
3 Discuss the statement: Enzymes have a binding site that is substrate-specific.
An increase in temperature can speed up enzyme-catalysed reactions, but only to a point.  
When heated too much, enzymes, because they are proteins, become denatured.

When you see the symbol shown in figure 1 in an equation, it signifies that the reaction  
involved is an equilibrium reaction. 
equilibrium reactionS:
• Convention has the reactants shown on the left and the products on the right.
• The reaction proceeding from left to right is called the forward reaction.
• The reaction proceeding from right to left is called the reverse reaction.
•  When the reactants are mixed, the reaction initially goes in the forward direction.
•  Once some products are formed there will be a simultaneous reaction going in the reverse direction.
•  After a period of time, the rate of forward reaction and the rate of the reverse reaction will be equal. The reaction 
is then said to be in equilibrium.
•  At equilibrium, there is a specific ratio of reactants to products.
•  At equilibrium, the mixture usually consists almost entirely of products (position of equilibrium lies to the right) 
or almost entirely of reactants (position of equilibrium lies to the left), depending on the specific reaction.
•  Whether you start with the reactants or products of a particular reaction, the system will eventually reach the 
same position of equilibrium.

this context.

Explain what this means.

yield as much product as possible. Knowledge of how equilibrium systems react to change is essential for dealing

The word organic is often used to imply that a product is ‘natural’ or better than other, similar goods. Organic 
vegetables are produced without the use of pesticides and cost more than other vegetables. Originally a compound 
was only considered to be organic if it was only produced by an organism. In chemistry, ‘organic’ has a different 
meaning – it applies to carbon-based compounds with the exception of oxides and carbonates.

Carbon is only the 14th most abundant element on Earth. However, there over 10 million organic compounds, many 
times more than in any other class of compounds. There is a huge variety in the size, shape, physical properties 
and chemical properties of these componds. This is due to a combination of factors. Carbon is in Group IV of the 
Periodic Table and is tetravalent.

Carbon’s ability to form up to four strong covalent bonds at different angles means it can form  
branching molecules. Carbon also exhibits concatenation – the formation of long chain molecules  
based on a ‘backbone’ of carbon atoms.
4 Silicon is the other element that can display concatenation.

There are many organic molecules so it is important for there to be a system 
in place to help chemists accurately name and identify these molecules. The 
International Union of Pure and Applied Chemists (IUPAC) has developed 
nomenclature for organic compounds, based on their structures. Many organic 
compounds also have ‘trivial’ (common) names from the time before the 
IUPAC system was established. 
In the IUPAC system, alkanes (and other organic compounds) are named using a prefix and a suffix. The prefix tells 
us the number of carbon atoms. The suffix (-ane) tells us that the compound is an alkane; i.e. a hydrocarbon that has 
only carbon-to-carbon single bonds. The first four prefixes (meth-, eth-, prop- and but-) were assigned prior to their 
structure being known. Prefixes after this are derived from Greek numbers.
Table 1 shows the basis for naming hydrocarbons and  
other organic compounds.

halogens replace hydrogen in alkanes, the resulting compounds are 
called haloalkanes (IUPAC nomenclature) or alkyl halides.

from the Latin term acetum, meaning ‘vinegar’. Household vinegar is about 7% ethanoic acid  
dissolved in water.

Quantitative analysis uses solutions of known concentrations to calculate  
the concentrations of other solutions. An essential part of a quantitative 
analysis is a primary standard. This is a substance that is used to make a 
solution of very accurately known concentration. This in turn is used to  
make other standard solutions.
In order for a substance to be suitable for use as a primary standard, it must:
• be available in a pure form 
• be very soluble in water
• react with desired substances
• be stable – not react with substances present in air, i.e. oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour
•  not change mass while being weighed, eg by losing water to the atmosphere (efflorescent) or gaining water from 
the atmosphere (hygroscopic). 
In addition, it is desirable that the substance has a high molar mass so that errors in weighing make as small a 
percentage difference as possible.
1 
Suggest one other advantageous property of a substance used to make a primary standard.
Common primary standards include:
• Sodium carbonate, Na2CO3
• Potassium dichromate, K2Cr2O7
• Hydrated copper sulfate, CuSO4.5H2O

A typical traffic accident
2
S P E E D
A N D
A L C O H O L
2-12
It was a Friday evening when the fatal accident
occurred. Andy Allen was an Agricultural
Chemicals salesman who spent a lot of his
work
time
travelling
throughout
the
countryside visiting farmers with samples of his
firm’s product. His job was to persuade farmers
to
buy
his
company’s
drenches,
feed
supplements and other products. His car was a
recent model and he appreciated its comfort as
he spent a lot of his day sitting in it as he
travelled from farm to farm.
Andy had been away from home the whole week. He was tired and looking forward to getting home
to spend the weekend with his wife and young daughter. It had not been a good week. The farmers
were not keen to spend money trying new products and, on top of that, he never slept well in strange
motels. As he was driving towards home, he was thinking about what he could do next week to try
to improve his sales figures because his boss had been hassling him about it.
The road he was travelling on was a major one between two large towns. The road surface was quite
new and Andy was making good time. He had only about another 100 kilometres to go, so estimated
that he would be home in about another hour. He decided to ring his wife on his mobile phone to
let her know the time he expected to be home. With annoyance and impatience he found that he was
catching up to a large slow truck on the hills. As well as that, it had just started to drizzle, so he had
to put his windscreen wipers on.
Belinda Brown was on her way home on the same road, but travelling in the opposite direction. She
was thankful that it was Friday. She worked in the local solicitor’s office in the large town that she
had just left behind. She lived with her husband and four-year-old son on a small property about
20 kilometres out of town. It was 6.30 pm, and just starting to get dark. Jason, having been picked up
from childcare, was whining from the back seat, as he was tired and hungry.

crumple zones
2
S P E E D
A N D
A L C O H O L
2-8
While compulsory seat belts have had a big effect on reducing the road toll, it was felt that even more
could be done. Over recent years two new technologies have been developed to give additional
protection to people who find themselves involved in a road accident. What was needed was for the
body to be cushioned so that it could come to rest a little more slowly.
An air bag inflates in only a fraction of a second so that a person moving forward into their seat belt
is cushioned before their head can reach the hard obstructions in front of them.
The other new feature that most new cars now have is what is called a ‘crumple
zone’. This means that during a collision, the front part of the car is designed so
it will slowly crumple up, taking much of the force of the collision.
The passengers are held safely in a stronger compartment
that stays intact but will come to rest more slowly as the
front of the car takes much of the force.
The following activity will help you understand how
the idea of a crumple zone works.

Alcohol and driving
2
S P E E D
A N D
A L C O H O L
2-13
The substance we commonly call alcohol is the chemical
ethyl alcohol or ethanol. Its chemical formula is
CH3COOH, and it is found in nature in fermented fruit.
Fermentation is where sugars in the fruit, combined with
natural fungi like yeast, cause a chemical reaction,
which produces ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide gas.
Alcohol is a depressant. It slows a person’s reaction time
and can distort his or her judgement of speed and
distance. It also reduces a driver’s ability to concentrate.
The more a person drinks, the greater the effect. For this reason, throughout Australia, if a person
has a full driver’s licence, the maximum blood alcohol concentration (BAC) is 0.05%. This means
that there is 0.05 gram of alcohol in every 100 millilitres of blood.
Once alcohol is in the body, it can only be removed by being broken down in the liver. This process
takes time. The liver can only break down about 8 grams of pure alcohol, or one standard drink, per
hour. Nothing, including drinking strong black coffee, cold showers or sleeping it off, can speed up
this process. This means that once a person has reached the legal limit, consuming one standard
drink per hour will keep them at that level.
A person’s level of alcohol is affected by both their weight and their sex. The lighter a person is, the
less alcohol is needed to put them over 0.05. Also, if the person has not eaten recently, because
alcohol is absorbed more quickly if the stomach is empty, the effect may be greater.
As a general guide, women should think carefully before their second drink, because two standard
drinks in the first hour may put many women over the legal limit. Men are likely to go over 0.05 if
they have a third drink in their first hour.
What is a standard drink?

Blood groups
1
B L O O D
A N D
D N A
1-2
Before the 1900s, it was well known that if blood from one person came in contact with the blood of
another person, very often the red blood cells would form clumps and so no longer be able to carry
out their role.
In 1901, Austrian biologist, Karl Landsteiner, discovered that some people had certain antigens that
could affect blood that did not have that antigen. The different blood types were named A (if it had
only antigen A), B (if it had only antigen B), AB (if it had both A and B antigens) and O (if it had
neither A nor B antigens). It was found that these blood types contain antibodies that react against
the antigens as shown in the table below.
Every living person belongs to one of these four blood groups; the group being decided at the
moment of conception and inherited from the parents. Hence the blood group is fixed for life and
does not change. This ABO system of blood grouping interests forensic scientists because even if
dried, the antigens can be detected and identified.
Nowadays the technique of DNA profiling can use blood to link a specific individual to a bloodstain.
However, even before this development, a blood sample was considered important evidence if found
at a crime scene.
Blood is a good example of a class characteristic because it is associated with a group of people all
having the same characteristic (ie the same blood group). It is not unique to only one individual, like
a fingerprint. Such evidence is still very important during investigations because it eliminates some
suspects and so decreases the number of people who need to be examined further.
This type of evidence allows the calculation of the probability that a sample of blood found at a crime
scene came from a particular person. To do this, the proportion of the population belonging to that
group or class needs to be known.

Blood splashes
1
B L O O D
A N D
D N A
1-4
Examination of blood splashes and smears at a crime scene is an essential part of a murder
investigation. The position and appearance of blood marks on the body and surroundings will help
the investigator to reconstruct the crime.
For example, because blood cannot flow uphill against gravity, it may indicate to the investigator that
a body was moved after the victim was killed. French criminologist, Alexander Lacassagne, is
credited with linking the shape of blood spots with the position of the victim.
Blood dropped vertically, onto a stationary, flat surface forms
a circular mark with a serrated edge. (see right)
Drops of blood falling from a moving object hit a flat surface
at an angle, leaving a spot like an exclamation mark, with a
smaller spot showing the direction of movement. (see right)
The arrow shows the way the person was moving.
It is sometimes possible to make a rough
estimate of the height from which blood
fell by inspecting its edges. As the height
increases, so does the length of the spines
or serrations. (see right)
Examination of the shape of obliquely falling blood
splashes yields information about the direction and speed
of impact. Such evidence helps to determine the
positions of the victim and assailant at the time of the
assault and may indicate the degree of violence, the type
of weapon used and which person was the attacker and
who was in a position of self-defence.
The shape of the blood splashes is approximately related
to the steepness of the angle of fall. (see right) The
thickness of the blood, due to the degree of clotting, also
has some affect on the shape.
Blood smears tend to start as drops, which become
ragged at one edge, indicating direction of travel of the
smear. (see right) The arrow shows the direction in
which the blood was smeared.
When a bloodied surface, like hair, is brushed against a
clean surface a distinctive ‘swipe’ pattern results.

Case study: How blood splashes
exonerated an innocent man
1
B L O O D
A N D
D N A
1-6
A classic murder case in which blood evidence played a major, if controversial, part occurred in 1954.
Dr Sam Sheppard’s wife was found dead on a bed in an upstairs room of their home in Ohio, USA.
She had been hit by over 30 blows with a blunt object. The room had been ransacked, and was
heavily spattered with blood. A trail of stains led down the stairs and onto a terrace.
Dr Sheppard, who had been awakened from sleep
on the living-room sofa by his wife’s screams,
claimed to have been knocked unconscious by an
intruder as he rushed up the stairs to help his wife.
His behaviour was thought to have been suspicious,
and so there was some doubt about his story. This
was partly due to his infidelity towards his wife.
The doctor was sent for trial and found guilty of
murder. The coroner made much of the bloodstains
found on the pillow in the murder room and a
bloody imprint, which he suggested, was made by a
surgical instrument.
The murder room was full of blood splash evidence which if properly examined would have led to
other conclusions. A forensic expert in blood splashes examined the room several months later and
came to the following conclusions. As the ceiling showed no traces of blood, the murder weapon
must have been used almost horizontally. This was supported by the state of the blood splashes on
the walls, some of which appeared to be cast offs flung from the weapon as it was moved backwards
and forwards on to the victim’s head.
The investigator carried out experiments which suggested that the most likely weapon to have caused
the pattern of blood splashes was a heavy torch. He concluded, having noticed blood drops that had
been smeared into streaks on the right side of the victim’s bed, that the murderer had stood between
the twin beds. This suggestion was supported by blood-free areas on two of the walls behind the
murderer, which had been protected from flying blood by t

Braking distances
2
S P E E D
A N D
A L C O H O L
2-11
Friction
When brakes are applied, they rely on the grip of the
tyres on the road and the grip of the brake pads on the
tyres to bring the vehicle to a stop. Another word for
grip is friction, which is a force that resists movement.
Friction depends on the roughness of the two surfaces
that are in contact. The rougher the surfaces, the greater
the friction or grip.
Besides friction, two other factors that affect a car’s
ability to brake are its mass and speed. Generally, the
heavier a vehicle is, the more force that is needed to
bring it to a stop, and usually the longer it will take for
this to occur.
This can easily be understood if you
imagine a large truck, a medium car, a
small car and a motorcycle all travelling at
exactly the same speed. If they all have to
stop suddenly, it will take a much greater
force to stop the large truck than the
smaller vehicles. Now if the same force is
used, then it will take a much longer
distance to stop the truck than a car or
motorcycle.
Similarly, if two identical vehicles are travelling at different speeds, one at 20 km/h, the other at
60 km/h, then it is easy to understand that the faster car will take longer, or need a greater braking
force, to bring it to a stop.
This property, combining speed and mass, is called momentum.
Momentum = mass × speed
In most cases the exact mass of a car is not known. It has been found by testing, that an average
family sized car with good brakes, travelling on a dry road, will be able to reduce its speed by 7 m/s
to 8 m/s every second. This means that a car travelling at 60 km/h will take just over two seconds
to stop, after the brakes are applied.
Calculating braking distance
To calculate the braking distance, remember that:
distance = average speed × time
To calculate the average speed, find the mean of the initial speed and the final speed (zero).
average speed =
initial speed + final speed

DNA profiling
1
B L O O D
A N D
D N A
1-9
This is probably the most important discovery for use in forensic science since the development of
fingerprinting over a hundred years ago. While blood grouping can positively exclude a suspect, it
can only give a probability as to guilt. DNA profiling can actually prove a
person’s identity, except in the case of identical twins. No wonder it has been
said to have revolutionised crime solving.
It was in September 1984 at Leicester University, England, that Professor Alec
Jeffreys stumbled across his exciting discovery. He was working on parts of DNA
where there was a sequence of bases that varied greatly in unrelated individuals.
He and his team found a way in which these sequences could be made visible
as X-ray lines that looked a little like a bar code. These ‘bar codes’ give a unique
pattern for every person, hence the original term of ‘genetic fingerprinting’.
How a DNA profile was produced
1. A blood or hair sample is collected
from a suspect and a garment found
at a crime scene.
2. The DNA is extracted in the laboratory,
then ‘cut’ into small pieces using a
scissors-like chemical called an
enzyme. The lengths of these fragments
differ greatly from person to person.
3. Next these pieces are placed in a gel
through which an electric current is
passed. The current carries the
fragments along through the gel. The
shorter pieces move faster, so they end
up further along than the longer pieces.
4. A chemical is added that causes the
two strands of DNA to unlink like a
zipper being opened. The sorted DNA
fragments are now transferred to a
sheet of nylon.
5. Radioactive strands of DNA (called
probes) are added, and they link up
with some of the fragments. The rest
are rinsed away.
6. When the nylon sheet is placed under
some photographic film, the
radioactive probes expose it, and
when developed, they leave a pattern
that resembles a bar code.
7. This pattern of dark bands from the
suspect’s blood is compared to the
pattern ma

A N D
A L C O H O L

Being allowed to drive a vehicle on a public road is a privilege and not a right. Today a person
wishing to take a vehicle out on the road must have a current driver’s licence. To obtain such a
licence they have to pass a number of tests to show that they are competent at handling the vehicle,
and know the rules that govern the behaviour of all persons on the road.
Once a person has qualified and obtained
their licence they are expected to abide
by the rules. They should drive within
the speed limit set for the piece of road
that they are driving on, and be alert,
courteous and considerate of other road
users. They should not be under the
influence of alcohol or other drugs, which
will impair their judgement. If a driver breaks
these rules and is caught, then punishment usually follows.

uploads/science/Worksheets/Forensic Scie.searchText:
Inertia
2
S P E E D
A N D
A L C O H O L
2-7
The reason why a person keeps moving forward in a collision is the property of inertia. It means that
a body will continue moving in the direction it was going, or will remain at rest, unless it is acted on
by a force. This is also called Newton’s First Law of Motion.
This property is clearly seen if you are standing up
in a stationary bus. If the bus takes off suddenly,
your feet, which are attached to the bus floor, will
move forward with the bus because this force is
acting on your feet. However, the rest of your
body will try to remain behind where you were
and you feel as if you are falling backwards.
Now if the bus stops suddenly, again your feet,
which are in contact with the bus floor will stop,
but the rest of your body will attempt to continue
moving forward at the same speed, until your
legs, which are attached to your feet, pull your
body back. This means that you feel as if you are
falling forwards.
I? Questions
1. Why do you think all new cars now have headrests above the actual seats? Explain how they
should be adjusted and why.
2. Explain how whiplash injuries might occur. What can be done to avoid this injury?
3. Discuss why station wagon owners who carry heavy loads in the backs of their cars are advised
to have a strong grill between the back section and passenger compartment.
4. Some magicians are able to do a ‘trick’ in
which they give a tablecloth a very quick
tug such that the tablecloth is pulled out
from under the dishes, which are left
standing in their original places on the table.
Use the concept of inertia to explain how
this is done.
5. Describe, using the word ‘inertia’, what

Reaction distances
2
S P E E D
A N D
A L C O H O L
2-9
Factors affecting reaction time
In unexpected situations, such as the car in
front braking suddenly or a child or animal
running out onto the road, it takes some time
for the driver to react to the danger. The
situation must first be observed, then it takes a
certain amount of time for the message to reach
the brain, where it is processed, and then
another message is sent to the muscles of the
leg to contract and push on the brake.
The time from when the situation first occurred, up to the time the brakes were applied, is called the
reaction time. This time can be affected by a number of things, including tiredness and hence the
alertness of the driver, being under the influence of alcohol or other drugs, or being distracted by
things either inside the vehicle or outside it.
Calculating reaction distance
By rearranging the formula for calculating speed (v = ), the distance travelled can be calculated if
the speed is known.
ie
reaction distance = time taken to react × average speed
It has been measured under test conditions, that the average reaction time for an alert driver is about
0.75 seconds. However, in normal situations on the road, a driver will not be as alert as when he or
she knows he or she is being tested. Hence it is more realistic to assume a reaction time of about two
or three seconds.
Now using the formula above for calculating distance, we can easily work out how far the car will
travel in the time it takes the driver to react. For example:
What is the distance a car will move, while travelling at 60 km/h, when an alert driver takes
one second to react to a child who has run out onto the road?
Note: It is best to convert km/h to m/s (divide it by 3.6) so that calculations are easier and the
final distance will be in metres.
distance = time × speed
= 1 second × 60 ÷ 3.6 m/s
= 16.7 metres
Summary
Reaction distance depends on the alertness of the
driver and the speed at which the car is travelling.

A N D
A L C O H O L
2-5
It is not speed that kills or injures people, but the force of an impact
on their bodies when they collide with a stationary object. The greater
the speed, the greater the force of the impact, and so the more
dangerous it is for the person.
The compulsory wearing of seat belts was first introduced around Australia
in the 1970s and further extended in the 1980s. Before seat belt wearing was
made compulsory, extensive studies were done comparing the injuries
sustained in accidents by drivers who were wearing seat belts and those who
were not. The table below shows the results of one such study.
A survey of 20 000 drivers who were involved in car accidents was carried out to see how the
wearing of seat belts affected the type of injuries that were sustained.
Seatbelt webbing is made from special polyesters that must conform to very strict Australian
standards that include strength and ability to stretch under load then recover from the stretch. It must
also be resistant to sunlight degradation and abrasion. Tests are carried out to ensure all seatbelt
webbing meets these standards.

Why should there
be a speed limit?
2
S P E E D
A N D
A L C O H O L
2-4
Forces during a collision
During a collision, a person sitting in the vehicle comes under a tremendous force
that is very hard to imagine. The person’s body must slow from a driving speed of
possibly 60 km/h or more to zero in only a few seconds when the vehicle hits a
stationary body such as a tree or barrier.
This force is better understood when we use the analogy of a
car falling from the top of a tall building. The greater
the speed at which the collision occurs,
the greater the force needed to
stop the car, and the greater the
force on the person’s body. Hence
the higher the building we imagine
the car falling from.
The effect of speed on stopping distance
It takes only a few experiments in a car to see that the greater the speed of a vehicle, the longer the
stopping distance, and hence the greater the chance of an accident occurring.
When a moving vehicle needs to stop suddenly, the time it takes for it to actually stop depends on
two main things:
1. The reaction time, which is the time it takes a driver to observe a situation and react to it.
2. The braking time, which is the time it takes for the vehicle to actually stop once the brake has
been applied. So,
Stopping Time = Reaction Time + Braking Time

excellent brakes on a good road at a range of different speeds.

Although the forensic laboratory is not often involved

When an accident occurs, after any injured people

so that the cause of the accident can be determined.
Only then can it be decided if criminal charges need

then the investigation becomes a coronial inquiry.
Police records and statistics show that the two main
causes of road accidents are speed and alcohol.
After an accident, a number of photographs will be
taken and maps drawn to record the final resting
place of all the vehicles involved. Any eyewitnesses
to the incident will be interviewed, and the weather
and road conditions recorded.

What is blood?
1
B L O O D
A N D
D N A
1-1
Blood is probably the most important fluid that the forensic biologist has to deal with at a crime
scene. It makes up about 9% of a healthy person’s body weight, and the average adult has about
5 to 6 litres of blood in their body. When blood is spilt, it goes a long way and is extremely difficult
to remove completely. Murderers’ attempts to clean up usually fail because blood tends to stick to
clothing and the murder weapon, and is splashed around widely in a violent crime.
Blood found at crime scenes has trapped many killers who thought that they had removed all
incriminating traces. Tests for blood are so sensitive that they will show up the presence of blood
even after a surface has been wiped so that no blood is visible to the unaided eye. Blood that is many
years old can still be identified as blood and analysed for DNA.
Forensically, blood can yield a great deal of information. The first task for an investigator at a crime
scene is to determine whether any suspicious stains are blood by doing a presumptive blood test. If
the test is positive, then it must be determined if the blood is animal or human. Once this is
established, the stains can be further tested for approximate age, sex, blood group and now DNA.
Understanding how bloodstains and splashes appear under different circumstances can help
enormously in reconstructing the sequence of events in a violent crime. Bloody fingerprints, palm or
foot prints also tell their own story and may be very helpful in solving the crime.
Composition of blood
Blood is a very complex mixture. It consists of four main components: red blood cells, white blood
cells and platelets, all suspended in a pale yellow liquid called plasma.
Plasma consists of 90% water and 10% dissolved proteins, hormones salts, digested food materials
and waste products.
Red blood cells are a donut shape, and give blood its colour. They carry oxygen to the cells.
White blood cells are larger and less nume

What is DeoxyriboNucleic
Acid (DNA)?
1
B L O O D
A N D
D N A
1-7
DNA is a gigantic molecule found in the
nucleus of every cell and in every living
organism. It looks something like a ladder
with about 3 billion rungs, and is the
chemical that chromosomes are made of.
These are large entwined strands of DNA.
They can be divided into smaller sections
called genes, which are passed down from
parent to child. So the DNA from related
people is always more similar than DNA from
unrelated people. In the same way, the DNA of closely related animals and plants is also more alike
than the DNA of organisms that are only distantly related. It has been found that the DNA of the
primates has about 90% in common with the DNA of humans.
The only people who share exactly the same DNA are identical twins, because they started out as a
single fertilised egg, that in its early stages split apart, and then grew into two separate babies who
are genetically identical.
The legs of the ‘ladder’ consist of alternating molecules called sugars and phosphates (marked as ‘s’
and ‘p’ in the diagram above). The ladder twists itself into a ‘double helix’ to save room as it fits into
the nucleus. The rungs of the DNA ladder are made up of pairs of molecules called bases. There are
only four different bases, and they always pair up in exactly the same way:
adenine (A) always pairs with thymine (T), and cytosine (C) always attaches to guanine (G).
The DNA ladder has also been compared to a zip fastener with the four bases forming the teeth. The
difference is that in order to join the two strands of DNA, A must pair with T, and G must pair with
C. The order in which these bases appear is the genetic code that determines all inherited
characteristics (see below).
This DNA, or genetic code, is unique
to every person and is a combination
of which 50% is inherited from the
father and 50% from the mother.

like a zipper (see far right), and the
DNA copies this order of ba

What is speed?
2
S P E E D
A N D
A L C O H O L
2-3
Speed or velocity is a measure of how far an object moves in a certain time
period. The most commonly used units of speed are kilometres per hour
(km/h), or metres per second (m/s). A speed of 35 km/h is the speed
at which a vehicle would take one hour to cover 35 kilometres.
A speed of 10 m/s is the speed at which 10 metres is covered in
every second.
A speed given in m/sec can be converted to km/h by multiplying by
3.6. Similarly, km/h can be converted to m/s by dividing by 3.6.
Calculating speed
Speed can be calculated using the formula:
average speed =
This can be written in symbols:
v =
v = speed or velocity
Example: If you want to calculate the average speed of a car that travels 40 kilometres in half an
hour, you divide the distance (40 km) by the time (0.5 hours).
40 ÷ 0.5 = 80 km/h
To convert to m/s:
80 km/h ÷ 3.6 = 22.2 m/s

Ecosystems
Earth is a special place where organisms live in unique  
environments. The organisms require both living (biotic) and  
non-living (abiotic) components to survive. When two or more  
organisms live and interact with each other, they form a  
community. Each community lives in a specific area called a  
habitat. A habitat contains both biotic and abiotic features. Each  
specific area with its organisms is called an ecosystem.

Each plant and animal has a specific function or position within its community. This function or position is 
called a niche. Green plants produce their own food and so are called producers. Animals that eat producers 
are called consumers. There are several levels of consumer. First order consumers eat plants and are herbivores. 
Second order consumers eat animals and are carnivores. Top order consumers are also carnivores. When a 
plant or animal dies, it decays. The organisms that break down the plants or animals are bacteria, fungi, worms 
and other invertebrates. These organisms are called decomposers.

Joints
Your body has 206 bones which are linked by joints. This is your skeletal system. The bones work like levers 
to give more speed and power to your movements. The joints allow articulation (movement) of the bones. 
Ligaments hold the bones together.
Joints like the elbow and ankle allow movement backwards and forwards, like a hinge. The shoulder and hip 
areas are ball and socket joints that allow rotation. The wrist allows movement in an ellipse in two directions, 
while the foot bones glide past each other on the same plane. The atlas and axis at the top of your neck allow 
you to pivot your head in most directions.

Keys and kingdoms
Animals and plants are so numerous that people need to classify them into groups and then into smaller groups 
to be able to talk about them. The groups are written in order of size, with the largest group first: Kingdom, 
Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species.
There are four main reasons for classifying into groups:
Communication – 
 
»
So I can say to you the word ‘marsupial’ and you will know I mean a furry, warm, 
pouched mammal.
Conservation 
 
»
– If we know how many there are of a group and we see the numbers declining, we can take 
action to make sure they survive into the future.
Ordering – 
 
»
This happens so we know which ones came first and we can find things, like all the books in a 
library or all the files on your computer.
Relationships – 
 
»
These show which organisms are related to each other. For example, the platypus and 
echidna are both monotreme mammals.

Natural resources

and general prosperity of a country or region as a result of the widespread development of mineral resources 
like coal or uranium. Western Australia is experiencing a huge resources boom in iron at the moment. In the 
1850s there was the goldrush in Victoria when 370 000 immigrants arrived in Australia and the economy of the 
nation boomed.
We can get natural resources from the ground, the air, the water or plants. All the minerals and ores in the 
ground are natural. Humans make many products from these natural resources.

Solar system
Our solar system is made up of a medium-sized star called the Sun, eight planets, an asteroid belt and a comet 
belt. The four planets closest to the Sun are made from rock. The other four planets are called gas giants and are 
made up of various gases, but mainly hydrogen, helium, methane and ammonia. Mercury has no atmosphere 
while Venus and Mars have atmospheres made up of carbon dioxide. Earth’s atmosphere is made up of 
nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide and other gases. 
Mercury and Venus do not have moons and Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and Uranus do have moons. 
The moons are called satellites because they orbit their planet. All moons rotate. The Sun rotates every 27 days. 
Each planet rotates at a different speed on its own axis. All of the planets orbit the Sun in the same plane and 
their orbits are elliptical. The distance from the Sun to the Earth is 150 million kilometres, which equals  
1 astronomical unit (AU).

Atoms
There are four distinct models for representing atoms: the billiard ball model, the plum pudding model, the 
planetary model and the shell model.
John Dalton in 1803 developed the concept that pure substances were made of indivisible solid particles called 
atoms. John Joseph Thomson in 1897 discovered negatively charged particles that he called electrons. His 
model was the plum pudding model. In 1911, Ernest Rutherford discovered the small positive nucleus, which 
was surrounded by electrons. Niels Bohr in 1913 proposed that the electrons were arranged in layers around 
the nucleus and that this arrangement accounted for the chemical and physical properties of the atom.

All of the chemicals you use are formed when atoms react with each other. Knowing how atoms are organised 
is the basis of chemistry and enables you to make your own compounds.
The atomic number of an atom is found by counting the number of protons in the nucleus. Protons are 
electrically positive particles. The number of protons equals the number of electrons in an electrically balanced 
atom, so an element with an atomic number of 5 has 5 protons and 5 electrons. The neutral particles in the 
nucleus are called neutrons. The number of neutrons and protons makes up the mass number of the element. 
Electrons are arranged in shells. The first shell can have only two electrons. The second, third and fourth shells 
can have up to 8 electrons.

Biotechnology
Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or other biological systems in a technological field. 
Uses of biotechnology include the manufacture of drugs, environmental management such as waste recycling, 
the use of genetically engineered bacteria to produce human hormones and the production of genetically 
modified crops.

It appears that yields from GM crops such as canola are generally higher, so a farmer may earn more money

DNA
DNA has a pattern for every living organism and is specific to an individual, for example, you. DNA can be 
used to determine relationships such as the parentage of a child, and to provide clues at crime scenes. DNA 
molecules are made of smaller chemical units called nucleotides. Without the nucleotides, there would be no 
DNA nor would you exist. 
DNA has all the instructions to make and shape your body. DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid, and it was 
discovered in the 1860s by Friedrich Miescher. However, it wasn’t considered important until Rosalind Franklin 
demonstrated through X-ray crystallography photographs that DNA had a helical structure. Watson and Crick 
pursued the concept and looked at the structural function of DNA. They showed that DNA was also a method 
of copying genetic information. 
1 
Using an example, explain the advantage of exact dNA replication.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
DNA is found in the nucleus of the cell, which is the cell’s control centre. 
Chromatin has genetic material and is composed of DNA and a protein. At 
certain stages of the cell’s life, the chromatin condenses into chromosomes 
prior to replication of the cell. 
2 
in the box at the right, draw a diagram of a cell showing the nucleus and 
chromosomes that it contains.
Inside the double helix structure of DNA are the bases adenine (A), thymine 
(T), cytosine (C) and guanine (G). Adenine and thymine form two hydrogen 
bonds to each other while guanine and cytosine form three hydrogen bonds to 
each other. This means that A always bonds with T, and C with G. 
The outer structure is made from sugar–phosphate 
units. The sugars are connected to the four bases.

Earthquakes
The edges of tectonic plate boundaries are rough and jagged and have many faults in them. As the plates move 
against each other, they get stuck and pressure on the boundary or a block increases. When the force of a block 
or plate boundary is suddenly released the stored energy radiates out in all directions. The energy is released as 
seismic waves. These waves shake the ground and anything on it!
Earthquakes generate compression, transverse and longitudinal waves – that is, P, S and L waves. The amplitude 
or height of the S waves determines the magnitude of an earthquake. Scientists calculate the magnitude using a 
time–velocity graph. The magnitude is the measure of the amount of energy released by the earthquake. 
The time is calculated by subtracting the P wave from the S wave as they arrive at the seismic station, and is 
measured in seconds. The amplitude of the S wave is measured in millimetres. 
1

a magnitude 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
        
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
b Seismic wave  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
        
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
c Amplitude 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
        
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The strength of the earthquake is based on a logarithmic scale – the Richter scale. An increase of one unit in 
the Richter scale represents a ten-fold increase in the amplitude of the seismic wave. Using the information 
from different seismic stations, the location and depth of an earthquake can be calculated. This process is called 
triangulation.

Electricity
Charge
Electricity is a form of energy that has physical properties related to the force and motion of electrically charged 
particles – the electrons. Neutral objects have equal numbers of protons and electrons.

electrical ‘earth’ is anything that can give up or take on an unlimited amount of charge, such as the ground. 
When an object becomes charged, –ve (negative) electrons are added or removed.

Fossils
Fossils are formed from the hard parts of a shell or a skeleton. With plant fossils, it is usually the leaves and the 
woody parts that are found. Fossils can form as impressions, moulds and casts. They can be found in amber (a 
plant resin), ice and sedimentary rocks such as coal, shale and sandstone. Fossils provide important evidence of 
past life, and relate the evolution of organisms.
1 
explain why fossils found in rocks are usually found only in sedimentary rocks.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The process of fossilisation takes time. When an organism dies and falls into soft sediments, such as those 
found in lakes and ocean floors, the soft parts usually decay very quickly, leaving only the hard parts. The 
processes of fossilisation are: mineralisation, replacement, re-crystallisation. Moulds and casts can be formed.
2 
Write these words in the correct order to summarise the process of fossilisation: mineralisation, death, 
sediment burial, replacement, decay, compaction.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The remains of the organism become compacted and mineralised, and eventually the layer turns to rock. The 
rock layer eventually becomes exposed.
3 
The largest herbivorous dinosaur in Australia was recently discovered in Queensland. The fossil was embedded in 
sandstone. describe how this dinosaur was fossilised.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Fossils are found in rock layers. The oldest fossils are in the deepest rock layer while the youngest fossils are 
found in the layers nearest to the surface. This is the basis of the Law of Superposition.
4 
explain why more advanced fossilised organisms are found in younger rocks.

Hormones and nerves
Hormones are chemical messengers made by endocrine glands. These glands secrete hormones directly into 
the circulatory system. Each hormone has a specific chemical function and is received by specific target cells 
causing a specific bodily response. The pituitary gland is called the master gland. It is about the size of a pea, 
and found at the base of the brain. The pituitary secretes stimulating hormones such as luteinizing hormone 
(LH), follicle stimulating hormone (FSH), adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), and thyroid stimulating 
hormone (TSH). The pituitary produces growth hormone and antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
Luteinizing hormone triggers ovulation in females, and in males triggers the production of testosterone and 
the manufacture of sperm in the testes. Follicle stimulating hormone stimulates the early maturation of ovarian 
follicles, and in males the production of mature sperm. ACTH targets the adrenal glands that sit on top of the 
kidneys to produce steroids. ACTH is also necessary for the production of the sex hormones oestrogen and 
testosterone. Progesterone is essential for the maintenance of pregnancy and the proper functioning of the 
menstrual cycle. Progesterone is found in both males and females as it assists with raising body temperature.

Indicators and pH
Indicators are used to find out if a substance is acidic or basic. They are dyes that can be derived from various 
plants such as nasturtiums, red cabbages and hibiscus flowers. In the year 1300, Villanova discovered that 
lichens can be used to make litmus paper. Blue litmus paper turns red when dipped in acid and red litmus 
paper turns blue when it is dipped into a base. Not all chemicals react with litmus paper; for example, chlorine 
gas bleaches litmus paper white. 
Indicators such as universal indicator paper contain many dyes that 
change colour gradually over a wide pH range. Other indicators such as 
bromophenol blue, phenolphthalein and methyl red are very specific in 
their ranges. The table at the right shows some indicators and their pH 
ranges. Indicators are used for testing soils, pool water, bodily fluids and 
other chemical substances.
pH is the logarithmic scale of the hydrogen ions (H+) in a solution. A pH 
of 0 is strongly acidic, and a pH of 14 is strongly basic (OH–). A neutral 
pH is 7. 
The pH level varies in bodily functions. The human stomach has a pH 
of 1 because it produces hydrochloric acid. Other parts of the digestive 
system have a higher pH. Human blood has a pH of 7.3–7.5. If these 
levels are exceeded in either direction, the body cannot process properly 
the ingested foods and gases.

Joules, watts, amps and volts
Joules are a measure of energy. You use energy every day and you need to maintain a level of energy to keep 
you functioning, even while you sleep. Every action you do expends energy. 
James Prescott Joule was an English physicist, born in 1818 in Salford, Lancashire. Joule studied the nature of 
heat, and discovered its relationship to mechanical work. He also stated that heat is a form of energy. This led to 
the theory of conservation of energy. The joule is the international scientific unit for measuring energy.
1 
What do you think the theory of conservation of energy is?
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Think of a joule as the energy used when a 100 g mobile phone is lifted through a height of 1 metre and held 
against the force of gravity, which is almost 10 Newtons. One joule is defined as the amount of energy exerted 
when a force of one Newton is applied over a displacement of one metre. A joule is also the equivalent of one 
watt of power being radiated for one second. This means that the energy in food can be related to the amount 
of work that can be done from specific food items. Food energy is commonly measured in kilojoules (kJ).
2 
A chocolate biscuit has 300 kilojoules of energy. How many times must a 100 kg person walk up a 5 m high stair 
case to use up this energy? (Assume the force of gravity = 10 Newtons)
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Consider a 9 volt battery with a current of 1 amp. This means that 9 joules per second (or 9 watts) are being 
used. When one joule is used per second, the unit of power is called a watt, after James Watt. One watt of power 
is equivalent to the rate at which energy is produced by a candle. Think of a watt as a quantity of electrical 
energy flowing per second. The amount of power being used is the rate at which energy is expended, or  
Power = Volts x Amps, which can be written as P = VI.

Motion
Speed is the word we use to describe how fast an object is moving. Speed is calculated by the distance travelled 
divided by time. In science, it is measured in metres per second. The equation for speed is:
Velocity is not the same as speed. Velocity does describe how fast an object is moving, but it also describes the 
direction in which the object is moving. Therefore a change in the direction of an object is a change in velocity, 
but not necessarily a change in speed. Velocity is calculated the same way speed is, but the units are usually in 
metres per second plus direction, e.g. 30 ms–1 east.
Acceleration is the change in the velocity of a moving object, and can refer to an increase in velocity or a 
decrease (negative acceleration). The equation for acceleration is:
The units are expressed in metres per second per second or ms–2. 
Acceleration is directly related to Newton’s Law: Force = mass × acceleration.
Note: For the following questions, convert all distances to metres and all times to seconds.

Motion is often represented with graphs. The steeper the gradient, the faster the acceleration or deceleration. A 
horizontal line indicates that the object is moving at a constant rate.

Natural events
Volcanoes have provided the Earth with its atmosphere, water vapour and materials to make productive soils. 
Volcanoes also alter climatic conditions, because the volume of ash that is put into the atmosphere reduces the 
amount of the Sun’s radiation. The Mt Pinatubo eruption in the Philippines caused the temperature to fall one 
degree, inducing heavy rainfall. In Iceland, the Laki fissure volcanic eruption in 1783 caused Europe to have a 
prolonged cold spell for several years. Like cyclones, volcanoes can cause millions of dollars’ worth of damage.

pressure differences. The rain that is generated in a cyclone dilutes the upper layer of the sea and can affect the 
growth of corals. The rain also causes flooding and can kill animals that live in burrows as well as causing major 
erosion. The wind can cause damage to coral reefs and land vegetation as well as having an emotional effect on 
people. With climate change, cyclones will become more frequent and affect areas not usually prone to them.

Newton’s Laws
Basically, Newton’s Laws are intuitive – see that book over there? You’d get a shock if it moved all by itself. You 
expect things to stay in motion or motionless, unless acted upon by a force.
According to Newton’s First Law, an object will only change the way it is accelerating or moving if it is acted on 
by an unbalanced force, or not cancelled out by an equal force in the opposite direction. This means that objects 
will remain moving or stationary with the velocity they already have. In the absence of an unbalanced force, an 
object in motion will maintain its state of motion. This is often called the Law of Inertia. Inertia resists changes 
in its velocity.
1

Newton’s Second Law states that the acceleration of an object is dependent upon the unbalanced force acting on 
the mass of the object. That is, a large force = large acceleration, a small force = small acceleration. This concept 
can be expressed as:
acceleration = Force ÷ mass or a = F ÷ m 
force = mass × acceleration or F = ma

Non-renewable resources
Non-renewable resources are the fuels that cannot be replaced; for example, coal and oil, which were formed 
over millions of years. These fuels cannot be replaced in our lifetimes, so should be conserved carefully. 
The original source of energy for Earth is the Sun. The energy comes to Earth in the form of electromagnetic 
waves. Plants convert sunlight into carbon-based carbohydrates. In turn, the plants provide energy to the 
animals that feed on them.
Coal is formed when layers of buried plant material are compressed and altered. Oil is formed from large 
amounts of small marine organisms that have been buried for millions of years.
We burn oil in our cars as petrol and in planes as kerosene. Industry burns coal to produce electricity. Heat 
from coal is also used to produce metals, and coal is used to remove the oxygen from the metal ore.

Nuclear fission and fusion
Fission
Nuclear fission is valuable as it is used in atomic power plants, warships and nuclear weapons. The particles in 
an atomic nucleus are held together by a very strong force. When a neutron is fired at the nucleus, the atom 
splits into two or more new products, breaking the atom down and releasing energy for people to use. This is 
called fission or splitting. Not all nuclei undergo fission.

Periodic Table
Dmitri Mendeleev devised the Periodic Table, and it was first published in 1869. The 
table is divided into eight columns called groups and rows called periods. The groups 
are numbered from 1 to 8, and these numbers refer to the number of electrons in the 
outermost shell of each element. Each outer electron shell can hold a fixed number of 
electrons. Group 1, which is very reactive, has 1 electron. Group 7 has seven electrons and 
is also very reactive. Group 8 has eight electrons and the elements do not react readily, if at 
all. Each period is also numbered and tells you how many electron shells there are in each 
row. 
The electronic configuration of an element is written by the number of electrons in 
each shell, e.g. 2.8.3. The configuration tells you that the element is in Group 3 from 
its outermost shell with 3 electrons and that it is in the third row of the Periodic Table 
because there are 3 shells of electrons. This identifies the element as aluminium.

number of protons in the atom is equal to its atomic number. The higher the atomic number, the further it is

Quasars and stars
Quasars are the brightest and most distant objects in the known universe. They burn with the energy of a 
trillion suns and are a strong source of radio waves, which are detected by radio telescopes. Quasars are not 
true stars. The word ‘quasar’ means quasi-stellar radio source. Quasars have a very high red shift, which means 
they are moving away from the observer very quickly. The nearest quasar to Earth is 10 billion light years away.
1

b What conclusion does the red shift of the quasars suggest about our universe?
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Nebulae are gigantic gas clouds and are the basic building blocks of the 
universe. They contain the elements from which stars and solar systems 
are built. Nebulae are composed of about 90% hydrogen, 10% helium and 
0.1% heavy elements such as carbon, nitrogen, magnesium, potassium, 
calcium and iron.
2

A pulsar is formed when a massive star collapses and exhausts its supply 
of fuel. It blasts out in a giant explosion known as a supernova. If the 
mass of the core of the collapsing star is 1.4 times the mass of the star 
itself, it forms a neutron star. If it is less than this, it becomes a white 
dwarf. If the mass of the core is greater, a black hole results.

Reflection and refraction
Light travels in straight lines, but it can be bounced (reflected) back on an angle, depending on the angle of the 
surface that it strikes. The ray of light that strikes a surface is called the incident ray. The ray that is reflected 
from the surface is called the reflected ray. If a ray strikes the surface at 90°, it is called a normal ray. 
The Law of Reflection states that when a ray of light reflects off a surface, the angle of incidence is equal to the 
angle of reflection.

Tsunamis
‘Tsunami’ is a Japanese word meaning harbour wave. Now tsunami refers to a large water mass that has a very 
high energy level, and causes devastation in low-lying areas. The waves are in series, much like the ripples sent 
out by a pebble dropped into a pond. Earthquakes on the seafloor cause tsunamis. These earthquakes result 
from plate movement. The sudden slippage causes the water to travel away from the seismic event. Underwater 
landslides, land slumping into the ocean, volcanic eruptions, nuclear testing underwater and meteorite impacts 
can also generate tsunamis. The depth of the water controls the speed of a tsunami. As the wave approaches the 
land, the depth of the water becomes shallower and slows the wave – the rear of the wave is still in deeper water. 
This causes the water to build up height as well as ‘sucking’ the water from the shoreline.

Universe formation - theories
There are several different theories about how the universe began. The Big Bang theory is currently the most 
accepted theory. It suggests that the Universe was originally concentrated into a single, very small ball. The 
early universe was so highly unstable that an enormous explosion occurred. This formed the galaxies and stars. 
Evidence to support this theory is based on the expansion of space, as shown by the redshifts of distant galaxies 
and cosmic background radiation.
Redshift is the increase in wavelength of electromagnetic radiation. It is an example of the Doppler effect, 
which shifts the wavelength of emitted light of celestial objects towards the red (longer) wavelengths indicating 
that the objects are moving away from the Earth due to the continuing expansion of the universe. Redshift 
is based on the visible electromagnetic spectrum as well as other parts of the spectrum such as gamma rays, 
x-rays and ultraviolet waves. In 1965, the astronomers Robert Wilson and Arno Penzias discovered cosmic 
background radiation and showed that this radiation was from the Big Bang.

theory.

in the future. Scientific calculations suggest that the universe is expanding, so in order to maintain the constant 
state described in the Steady State theory, matter must be continually being created. Einstein’s theory says that 
mass can be created from energy, as shown in the equation E = mc2. (Energy equals mass multiplied by the 
speed of light squared)

X-rays and atomic particles
X-rays
Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen discovered X-rays in 1895. The rays were called X-rays because they were an 
unknown radiation that came from a vacuum tube. X-rays are produced when a high speed stream of 
electrons strikes the anode in a cathode ray tube. X-rays are the part of the electromagnetic spectrum that has 
wavelengths between 0.3 and 0.03 nanometres. They have very high energy. Many objects in space such as black 
holes, supernova remnants and stars emit X-rays. X-rays are also used to detect broken bones and damaged 
tissues in the body. X-ray detectors collect photons (a unit of electromagnetic radiation) of X-ray light, which is 
useful in astronomy. This collection has to be done in space as the Earth’s atmosphere stops their penetration. 
1

b What can happen if x-rays are absorbed by organisms?
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Gamma rays
Gamma rays (γ) have the smallest wavelengths, ranging from 0.03 to 0.003 nanometres, and have the most 
energy of any other wave in the electromagnetic spectrum. Henri Becquerel discovered gamma rays and 
beta particles. Supernova explosions, nuclear fission, nuclear explosions, black holes and pulsars produce 
gamma rays. Because of their short wavelengths, gamma rays can kill living cells. Gamma rays are used to 
sterilise hospital equipment that would be damaged by heat. Both gamma rays and X-rays are part of the 
electromagnetic spectrum.

Y chromosomes
If you are a female, you have two X chromosomes. If you are a male, you have an X chromosome and a Y 
chromosome. Von Nägeli first identified chromosomes in 1842. The word chromosome comes from the words 
chromo meaning ‘colour’ and soma meaning ‘body’. All organisms have chromosomes in their cells. 
Chromosomes are made up of DNA (Deoxyribonucleic acid) molecules, which carry the inherited 
characteristics called genes. The number of chromosomes varies in each species. Chromosomes are organised 
into pairs, and range from largest to smallest; this is called a 
karyotype.
1 
chromosomes carry different types and numbers of genes. 
Hypothesise why butterflies and kangaroos have such different 
numbers of chromosomes.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Sex chromosomes are the last two chromosomes, and are the 
smallest chromosomes.
All eggs carry an X chromosome, so the father determines 
the sex of the offspring, as sperm cells carry either an X or a Y 
chromosome. 
2 a draw a Punnet square to determine the sex of the offspring if a couple has four children.
b State the sex and percentage of the offspring.                                                                                                                                
The 45th chromosome in humans is the X chromosome. It often carries 
inheritable diseases which usually only affect males, such as haemophilia,  
red-green colour blindness and fragile X.
3 
determine the percentage of daughters and sons that are not affected by the 
inherited disease labelled xn. draw a Punnet square to help you find the answer.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The Y chromosome carries 2% of inheritable genes. Occasionally a male has an XXY condition, known as 
Klinefelter’s syndrome, where an extra X chromosome is inherited. People who suffer from this do not reach 
sexual maturity and are sterile. A similar condition called Turner’s syndrom

Zygote and reproduction
A zygote is the result of a sperm cell fertilising an ovum or egg. Reproduction in organisms can occur by 
budding, fragmentation, fission and spores. Fission occurs in bacteria and protozoa. Fragmentation occurs in 
planaria worms, budding in seaweeds and spores in ferns and fungi.

Australia’s environment
ESTUARY POLLUTION
A
s well as affecting coastlines and beachfronts, coastal degradation also 
happens in estuaries. An estuary is the part of the river near its mouth and 
is affected by the tidal movement of water. At high tide the sea water moves up 
the estuary and at low tide the fresh water moves out to sea. Pollution of the 
estuary is mainly due to sewage and stormwater runoff and can also include 
heavy metal pollution from industry. The pollution adds nutrients, pesticides, 
sediments, poisons and plastics to the drains, creeks and rivers and therefore 
to the water in estuaries. Contaminants often sink to the bottom of estuaries 
and remain for a long time in the sediment.

Animals such as prawns that live on the sediment take in pollutants as 
they feed. Bigger animals such as fish eat these small animals and the 
contamination becomes more concentrated. The last animal in the chain, 
the big carnivorous fish, are caught for human consumption and contain the 
poisons from all the small fish they have eaten. This can affect us.

Australia’s environment
F
eral animals are a major problem all 
around Australia and in particular the 
edges of the towns. This is where the natural 
environment is under greatest threat from 
humans. Many native animals including 
possums, birds, lizards, frogs and spiders are 
at threat from human pets and introduced or 
exotic animals and plants. When domestic pets 
escape or are abandoned they can turn feral 
and become very efficient killing machines in 
suburban bush areas. Some other examples of 
feral animals in Australia include: carp in the 
rivers, European green crabs off the southern 
coasts, wild pigs in the dry northern inland, 
foxes and deer in the eucalyptus forests and the 
most famous of them all, the rabbit.

• predator 
• carnivore
• suburban
Cats and dogs are well known for being 
carnivorous predators. When released into the 
wild, by accident or on purpose, these animals 
need to catch prey to survive and soon return 
to their instinctive hunting nature. The prey 
they can find mainly includes small native 
birds, frogs and lizards, but their diet can 
even include some species of kangaroo mice. 
Predation by feral pets is a major problem 
around the large cities.

in Australia.

describe what problems it may cause in 
our environment.

effect on our world over the next 5 to 10 
years, with the whole world being affected. 
Global warming is the name given to the 
gradual temperature rise over all the Earth. 
The change in temperature is small, perhaps 
only 2˚ to 3˚, but it will be enough to cause 
large amounts of polar ice to melt. This will, in 
turn, raise the sea level.

moving north, where it is cooler. This is one 
example 
of animals

to small

visual impact 
as well as

the Walter Hill

could affect 
tourism. People 
also believe it 
will be harmful 
to their health.

ater pollution results from rubbish 
and waste released into our rivers and 
oceans. We do not notice the pollution until it 
interferes with our use and enjoyment of the 
water so, unless our drinking water is dirty or 
the water in the creek is covered with an oily 
scum or the beach we swim at has rubbish and 
detergent froth in the waves or dead fi sh are 
found in the lake, we do not believe the water

Our Earth is unique in the Solar System 
because of its large amount of water - in the 
oceans, atmosphere, rivers and creeks and 
even the Arctic and Antarctic ice caps. Without 
water life could not exist on our planet. Most 
of the water is in the oceans but it is diffi cult 
to use because its high salt content. Fresh 
water is very limited and in some countries 
(including Australia) it is a scarce resource. 
Water therefore is very valuable and our use 
of water for drinking and washing, boating, 
fi shing and farming can all be threatened by 
pollution. The survival of the animals and 
plants that live in water and on its edges, such 
as in tidal pools and river banks, also depends 
on minimising the level of pollution in the

N
on-ionising radiation is found in the form of the energy waves in the 
electromagnetic spectrum. This spectrum is a label given to a large range 
of radiations each of which involves wave like (cyclical) changes to an electric 
charge together with corresponding changes to the strength of a magnetic 
field.
3f Non-ionising Radiation
Like any wave, electromagnetic waves have 
a specific frequency and wavelength. The 
wavelength (referred to as λ and measured in 
metres) is the distance between a particular 
part of a wave and the same part on the next 
wave. The frequency of the wave is defined as 
the number of whole wavelengths that pass 
a particular point per second. Frequency is 
measured in cycles/second or Hertz (Hz). All 
waves have the same relationship between 
wavelength, frequency and velocity. That 
is velocity equals frequency multiplied by 
wavelength. In a formula this is written as v = 
fλ. The energy of these waves is related to their 
frequency so the higher the frequency, the 
higher the energy.
1 
a 
A soccer field is 102 metres long. How 
long is that?
b 
What EMR wavelengths have the same 
length (or longer) than a soccer field?
c 
Approximately how long are the EMR 
waves which we detect as visible light?
d 
How can we detect: radio waves, infrared 
waves, light waves and x-rays?
e 
What is the frequency (hertz or cycles 
per second) of: microwaves, light, radar 
and gamma radiation?
f 
Which waves have the greatest energy?
For all electromagnetic radiation the velocity 
is the same as the velocity of light (3.0 x 108 
ms-1) and only varies when travelling through 
different substances, such as glass or plastic. 
In fact, visible light forms only a small part of

Radiation and safety
W
henever strong radiation affects living 
tissue the first effect is burning. The 
molecules in the cell cannot absorb the energy 
from strong radiation. Many thousands of 
chemical bonds are destroyed and the protein 
material in the cells and tissues is cooked. 
This has been most noticeable in the effects 
of atomic explosions in Japan and in radiation 
accidents in the former USSR and Japan.
It is generally accepted that low level radiation, 
such as diagnostic x-rays (when correctly used 
by radiographers to check bones and teeth) 
do not cause burning. This means that the 
exposure to the radiation is less than that 
required to physically destroy the body’s cells. 
It does not mean that the radiation is perfectly 
safe. 
3c Radiation and Health
There are two main types of radiation: ionising 
and non-ionising. Ionising radiation either 
adds or removes electrons to the material 
they contact whereas non-ionising radiation 
does not. Ions, or charged atoms, are made by 
changes to the numbers of electrons. Ionising 
radiation, such as gamma (γ) rays and x-rays, 
is produced from nuclear reactions, during the 
reaction as well as from radioactive material. 
This type of radiation is also found in very small 
amounts naturally in the environment. It is 
related to the ores of radioactive metals or as 
a part of solar energy. Non-ionising radiation 
is emitted by electronic equipment including 
power lines, telephone and radio transmitters 
and it is referred to as EMR or electromagnetic 
radiation.

Australia’s environment
S
ewage is full of raw nutrients returning 
to the environment. If sewage is returned 
close to urban areas the chance of disease 
spreading is high. The release of sewage into 
rivers also increases the chance of algal blooms, 
which cause oxygen to be reduced. An algal 
bloom happens when there is so much food 
that the algae grow very quickly. This means 
the available food and energy for other living 
organisms disappears and the area dies. Slow 
natural breakdown of wastes is required so 
that nutrients can be safely returned to the 
environment. Biochemical Oxygen Demand 
(BOD) is a measure of the quantity of dissolved 
oxygen used by organic matter under specified 
conditions. BOD can be used to predict the 
effect waste may have on fish or other aquatic 
organisms that require oxygen to live.

Australian Ecosystems
8e Biodiversity
Most Australia’s diverse wildlife is unique. 
About 80% of species occur only in Australia. 
This is because of the isolation of Australia 
over the last 150 to 200 million years. Recently 
introduced species are affecting these unique 
animals and plants. The most famous of these 
are the dingo (thousands of years ago) and, 
more recently, the rabbit and the cane toad.
Humans have been changing the Australian 
environment for the last 60 000 years but 
in the last century the rate of change has 
become much greater. Since 1788 almost 90% 
of woodlands and 50% of rainforest has been 
cleared and destroyed. This change has allowed 
soil erosion to destroy farming areas as well as 
the edges of the forests that remain.

B
iodiversity describes the variety of living 
organisms within an environment. This 
variety of life includes different plants, animals 
and micro-organisms. The number of species 
or different types of living things in the world 
is not exactly known but there are thought to 
be between 10 and 30 million different species 
on Earth. Many organisms that we do know of 
are not well understood. We don’t know how 
and where they live or how they interact with 
other species of organism or with us.
The number of different species in the world 
is being slowly decreased. This decreasing 
biodiversity is due to pollution and human 
intervention, such as hunting and logging. 
Native species continue to have their food 
eaten, or are killed themselves, by feral animals 
such as domestic cats and dogs that have 
escaped to the bush.

of the common mushroom. But, alas,

had that itchy feeling between the toes after 
showering in public showers? You may have 
had athlete’s foot, or tinea. Ever found an itchy, 
scaly mark on your skin that looks like a small 
circle? You may have had ringworm. Both these 
diseases are caused by fungi, but are also very 
easily cured in our society. 
Fungi are generally decomposers that break 
down just about any organic compound. Most, 
however, are parasitic and will break down 
the organic matter that is contained on living 
organisms, both plants and animals. The fungal 
cells secrete enzymes (organic catalysts) that 
promote digestion outside the cell, in this 
way large organic molecules are broken down 
into smaller molecules that the fungal cells 
can absorb and use. The fungi can reproduce 
using two main methods; sexual reproduction 
with the use of spores being produced by 
the hyphae, or, more commonly, via asexual 
budding or binary fission. Both of these

Disease is any altering of this state of wellbeing 
and involves the interfering of the normal 
functioning of the body. Some examples of 
disease include the flu, common cold, mumps, 
measles, chicken pox, cancer, Down syndrome, 
rickets, hepatitis, meningitis, AIDS. Diseases 
can be infectious or non-infectious.
Infectious diseases are diseases that are said to 
be contagious, ie they can be transmitted from 
one person to another via air, water or contact.

body, however they are not contagious and can 
be caused by a variety of means, for instance: 
• Nutritional diseases are caused by a lack of 
vital nutrients, eg vitamins or minerals. 
• Genetic disorders are due to the inheritance 
of genes that interfere with the normal 
functioning of the body, eg Down 
syndrome. 
• Environmental diseases occur where a 
chemical or something in our environment 
causes a disease, eg mercury poisoning or 
skin cancer due to exposure to the sun.

LOUIS PASTEUR (1825-1895)
Pasteur is remembered for disproving the 
theory of spontaneous generation. He did this 
by placing some broth in flasks as illustrated 
in the diagrams below. He heated this broth 
so that any organisms present were killed and 
the broth became sterile. He left the flasks 
and observed what happened. He noticed that 
the swan-necked flask remained sterile, while

organisms grew.

ROBERT KOCH (1843-1910)
Robert Koch was a German physician. He 
developed a method of identifying the micro-
organism that caused certain diseases. This 
method has been called Koch’s postulates.
Koch’s postulates
• The micro-organism that caused the disease 
must be present in all organisms suffering 
the disease.
• The micro-organism that caused the disease 
must be isolated in a pure culture.
• The micro-organism is injected into another 
organism (an experimental organism) and 
produces the same symptoms as the initially 
infected organism.
• The same micro-organism must be 
consistently isolated in pure culture from 
the experimental organism.

Australian Ecosystems
D
iversity of ecology is the range of different 
parts of the environment. An ecosystem is 
made up of the living communities of plants, 
animals and micro-organisms, as well as the 
non-living components such as soil, water 
and air, which are used as food and shelter for 
the living organisms. Some reasons for loss of 
biodiversity are shown in the diagram. Further 
explanation is given below.
8f Losing Our Biodiversity
• Clearing of native vegetation for either 
housing, forestry, mining or farmland 
encourages erosion and reduces the quality 
of the soil. In eastern NSW and Victoria 
over 90% of native vegetation has been 
removed.
• Introduced species can become 
competitors, predators or parasites on 
native wildlife. Many introduced micro-
organisms cause diseases to which native 
wildlife has no natural immunity.
• Poaching and the illegal trade in native 
wildlife is the modern-day equivalent of 
hunting. This can cause the destruction of 
large numbers of the most spectacular and 
rare of native species, birds and reptiles in 
particular.
• Pollution of the environment can destroy 
native plants or make it easier for 
introduced species to thrive. Either way the 
original native organisms are placed under 
further pressure.
