PACEMAKERS
At times the heart does not beat correctly. It is 
either too fast or too slow, and this is when the 
heart needs an artificial pacemaker. Pacemakers 
are small electronic devices that replace the 
sinoatrial node of the heart. They produce 
small electrical impulses that allow the heart to 
beat regularly. The general term of arrhythmia, 
or abnormal heart beat, can be classified into 
bradycardia (slowing of the heart beat) and 
tachycardia (speeding up and quickness of the 
heart beat).
The speed of the heart can determine the 
pressure in the heart. This is also affected 
by the width of the arteries (narrow or wide) 
through which the blood is pumped. When the 
ventricle relaxes the blood pressure reading 
is called diastolic, and the systolic pressure 
reading is when ventricles contract and blood 
is pumped into the arteries. Any change in 
the heart rate affects the flow of oxygen to the 
body and we could lose breath, become tired or 
show symptoms of lack of oxygen by parts of 
our body, in particular the lips and ends of the 
fingers, turning blue.

some have flagella, a tail-like structure that 
allows for movement, others have cilia, which 
are small hair-like projections. The third main 
type is called amoeba, which is a unicellular

no longer used. Instead positive pressure respirators or 
ventilators are used. These are a lot more compact and work 
differently to the negative pressure ventilator of the iron 
lung.

Educated at the College Mazarin in Paris, Antoine Lavoisier studied mathematics, astronomy, chemistry,
botany, and legal studies, His first job was to collect geological information for a map of France. Lavoisier’s
first published research was on the properties of the mineral gypsum. Later he was awarded a gold medal
by the King of France for research on street lighting. Lavoisier worked in a number of areas including the
Royal Gunpowder Administration and established the metric system of weights and measures. In 1793 he
was arrested by the leaders of the French Revolution because of his involvement in tax collection. Lavoisier
was executed by the guillotine.

The story so far

In 1597 the first chemical textbook Alchemia, by Andreas Libavius, was published. Alchemia or chemistry
was defined as the art of ‘producing reagents and extracting pure essences from mixtures. Many new
compounds were being prepared at this time by experimenting with animal and vegetable materials. Some
of these were alcohol, arsenic, zinc and three strong acids—hydrochloric, sulfuric and nitric. At this time
Georg Stahl (1660-1734) proposed the Phlogiston Theory as a way of explaining what happens when
substances burn or react with air, Substances that burnt easily such as coal were thought to contain large
amounts of phlogiston. (Phlogiston does not actually exist.)

Barbara McClintock was born in 1902 in Brooklyn, New York. As a student, she studied botany at Cornell
Univer graduating with her PhD in 1927. She later taught at Cornell before becoming a Professor at the
University of Missouri in 1936. Between 1942 and 1967, she did research on cytology (study of cells) and
genetics at a research laboratory in Cold Spring Harbour, New York. In 1983, McClintock was awarded the
Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine, one of only six women to have won this.

One of the most popular geological theories of the day was the theory of catastrophism. This theory stated
that most of the Earth’s history consisted of a short period of violent geological activity. This idea was based |
on some people's interpretation of Creation described in the Bible, Bishop James Ussher (1581-1656)
calculated that the Earth was created in 4004 BC. Because of this idea, most people believed the Earth had
only been in existence a few thousand years. These people thought that violent earthquakes, volcanoes and
floods had happened ‘all the time’, and created the world around them.

A totally different idea was developed by James Hutton (1726-97), a Scottish geologist. He thought the
world had been made some millions of years earlier and that changes had occurred much more slowly.
Lyell called Hutton’s theory uniformitarianism and supported it in his writings as strongly as he could.

what happens as particles are bombarded by other accelerated particles. All this led to increased
knowledge of the structure of the atom.

Flossie Wong-Staal (s.7-) 10a]

Flossie Wong-Staal’s original name was Wong Yee Ching and she was born in China in 1947. In 1952 her
family settled in Hong Kong. While at school, she was given the English name Flossie after Typhoon Flossie,
which had struck Hong Kong the week before. Wong-Staal enjoyed studying science and maths and her
family was very supportive of Wong-Staal continuing her education, In 1965, she emigrated to the United
States to study at the University of California, where she specialised in molecular biology and continued as
a postgraduate student in bacteriology.

After completing her doctorate she took a position with the National Cancer Institute in Bethesda,
Maryland, where she was the first researcher to copy the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). The
cloning of the virus that causes AIDS allowed Wong-Staal and other scientists to determine the structure of
HIV. She has continued to work in AIDS research, specifically gene therapy.

The story so far

In the 1970s, a number of rare cancers and other serious infections were becoming more and more common
in healthy people. Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome, or AIDS, was formally described in 1981 as a
syndrome. It was at first seen as affecting homosexual men, people who used intravenous drugs,
haemophiliacs, and some people who had been given blood transfusions. Today we know that specific
behaviours such as unsafe sex, the sharing of needles, or infection from blood, increases the risk of getting
| AIDs.

left school but he was still very interested in mathematics. Newton started at Trinity College in Cambridge
in June 1661. During one summer, the plague killed many people in London. Newton was sent to the
country for protection and while there he invented a new method of mathematical calculation. Later it
would be called calculus but Newton called it ‘method of fluxion’. It was based on finding the area under a
curve. Because of this remarkable piece of work, Newton was made Professor of Mathematics at
Cambridge when he was only 27 years old.

Nick Jacques was born in Walsall, England in 1949, and travelled to Australia in his youth. He studied both
chemistry and biochemistry at the University of Sydney, graduating with an Honours BSc in 1972 and a
PhD in 1977. Jacques’ thesis was on the relationship between bacterial surface structure and function. This
led him to research into oral microbiology. Jacques continues this research today in his positions as
| Principal Research Scientist at the Institute of Dental Research, and Head of Oral Biology at the University

of Sydney.

The story so far |

Since the first humans started to eat, their mouths have contained bacteria. These
bacteria come mainly from our mothers and close family members. The bacteria live on
particles of food and nutrients in saliva. In the mouth, bacteria attach themselves tothe |
» teeth to form coatings or biofilms known as dental plaque. These biofilms are responsible
for the two most common infections of humans—tooth decay, and gum and bone
diseases. Dental diseases cost Australians many millions of dollars annually in dental
services. More importantly they affect the health of millions of people, particularly
children. Jacques’ research career has been devoted to studying these oral bacteria.

‘having influence’. 
The flu is an infectious disease of birds and mammals caused by viruses 
of the orthomyxoviridae family. Huge flu epidemics affected the world in 
1918, 1957, 1968 and 1977. The pandemic of 1919 killed more than  
50 million people, which at the time was 2.5%–5% of the world’s

Stars
There are hundreds of billions of stars in the 
milky Way. Stars consist of 75% hydrogen, 22% 
helium and traces of oxygen, neon, carbon and 
nitrogen.
The nuclear fusion of hydrogen within the star provides the fuel for stars to 
release heat, light and energy. Stars are formed in nebulae, and most stars that 
we see are 1–10 billion years old.

Importance of stars

each aspect of society.
Stages in the life of a star
A star changes its shape and appearance 
throughout its life. The mass of a star is the 
principal determinant in its evolution and fate. 
When a star has exhausted its hydrogen supply, it 
burns helium and heavier elements which causes 
the star to expand and transform into a red giant. 
When the red giant loses enough fuel, its surface 
gravity causes it to collapse.
As pressure and temperature increase, the star can 
explode and become a supernova.

Chemical Reactions

WHAT IS A CHEMICAL REACTION?

Changes occur around us all the time. Bread goes dry, milk goes sour, steel nails rust, seeds sprout, water
evaporates and so on. We can classify these changes as either physical or chemical.

In a physical change, some of the properties of the substance change, but the substance is still the same.
For example, when liquid water is frozen and it changes to ice, its properties change. It is a now a solid
and cannot be poured — but it is still water. It still has the formula H,O (that is it contains two hydrogen
atoms and one oxygen atom per molecule) and can easily be changed back to liquid water by warming it.

1 What is the chemical symbol for hydrogen?
2 What is the chemical symbol for oxygen?

Ordinary light globes have thin coils of wire made of the metal tungsten (W) inside
them. These are called filaments. When electricity passes through a filament it
becomes white hot and gives out light (and heat), Even though it looks different,
the filament is still tungsten. This is a physical change because no new substance
has been formed. When you turn the light off, the filament is the same as it was
before you switched the light on.

A physical change can usually be reversed. In a chemical change new substances
are formed. Chemical changes are called chemical reactions and invariably involve

energy changes.

Burning is a chemical reaction. In a bushfire, vegetation is burnt, producing smoke and invisible gases,
and leaving ash (mainly carbon) behind. The smoke, gases and ash are new substances — they are
completely different from the original vegetation. The reaction also produces heat and light.

Another (slower) chemical reaction is the corrosion (rusting) of iron, Iron (Fe) is a shiny silvery metal and
it can combine with oxygen (0), a clear colourless gas, to produce Fe, O;.

Electricity |

Electricity is used to provide a versatile source of energy. It makes our lights work and, without it, we
wouldn't have radio, television, computers and CD players. We take electrical light globes (bulbs) for granted,
but they were only invented after a lot of hard work. Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor who
patented, in 1880, an electric light filament similar to those used in light globes today. Sir Joseph Swan (an
English scientist) came up with the idea for the incandescent electric lamp at the same time.

Electricity is the movement of electrons (negative particles) along a conductor. This flow of electrons is
called an electric current. For electricity to flow, it must have a complete pathway or circuit to follow. If
there is a gap, the circuit is broken and no current flows.

Energy can be stored in cells (sometimes called batteries) for conversion to

electrical energy when needed. Batteries are used when only low voltage (e.g. —j
3 volts to 12 volts) of electricity is used in calculators, watches and personal stereos

for example. Batteries are also used when things need to be portable. The first

battery was invented by the Italian Count Alessandro Volta in about 1800. The unit

of electrical measurement called the volt (V) was named after him.

Some electrical devices need large amounts of electricity to operate them. They are

powered by mains electricity (240 volts). Using batteries to supply large amounts

of electricity is not always practical — they would be too expensive and take up

too much space. Today people use a lot of electricity, at home and at work. This electricity is generated at

Inside the Earth

The Earth can be divided into four layers, The crust is the outer layer and it varies in thickness. It is
believed to be about 5 kilometres thick under the oceans. Under the continents it is thought to vary from
15 km to 35 km in thickness. The mantle is the next layer and it is about 2900 km thick. This layer is
believed to be semi-solid (like thick custard), The outer core is thought to be about 2200 km thick and made
of liquid rock. The inner core, which has a radius of approximately 1300 km, is believed to be solid,
probably iron (Fe) and nickel (Ni) under great pressure.
